source_site: YES - Youth Engineering Solutions (Museum of Science, Boston)
standards: Aligned to K-2 Computer Science standards (Data & Analysis; Algorithms & Programming) per publisher.
udl_rationale: action_expression: offers both a plugged (physical robot) and unplugged (peer-as-robot) pathway so students can show programming skill in the format that fits them; engagement: the real-world recycling/park cleanup story gives the coding task a concrete purpose
evidence: Students learn how to give instructions to a robot. They modify their programs to include repeating instructions to make it easy to tell the robot to do the same action several times.

title: Code & Go Robot Mouse Activity Set
description: A screen-free programmable robot mouse and maze set that lets K-2 students physically sequence directional coding cards to guide the mouse through a maze, building a tactile sense of algorithms before ever touching a keyboard.
subject: CS / STEM
materials: Code & Go Robot Mouse Activity Set (robot, maze grids/walls, coding cards) — physical kit sold separately
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to sequence directional coding cards to program a robot mouse through a maze.
Students will be able to debug a program by testing and revising the card sequence when the mouse takes a wrong turn.
price_note: Physical activity set must be purchased from Learning Resources; this page hosts a free accessible activity guide.
source_site: American Printing House for the Blind (APH) Tech — accessible guide for Learning Resources' Code & Go Robot Mouse
udl_rationale: action_expression: students physically place coding cards and watch the result immediately, a non-keyboard way to program; representation: directional arrow cards use symbols instead of text, accessible to pre-readers
evidence: Coding literally means the transformation of data into a form understandable by a computer-basically, telling a computer what you want it to do.

title: Thinking with KIBO: Introducing AI in Early Grades
description: A free 5-lesson curriculum that uses the screen-free KIBO robot to introduce early-elementary students to basic artificial-intelligence ideas, letting them snap together wooden coding blocks to test how a 'thinking' machine makes decisions.
subject: CS / STEM
materials: KIBO robot kit (sold separately); free printable curriculum guide
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to build a simple KIBO program using sequenced wooden blocks to represent a decision an AI system might make.
Students will be able to describe one way a computer/AI system 'senses,' 'thinks,' and 'acts' using their KIBO robot as an example.
price_note: The curriculum guide is a free download; using it fully requires a KIBO robot kit, sold separately.
udl_rationale: engagement: physically building and running a robot sustains attention better than a screen-based AI demo; action_expression: wooden block programming lets students test ideas by rearranging objects, not writing text
evidence: Early STEM education, where children learn at a young age about technology, computers, coding, and AI, is the key to giving children understanding and mastery of AI tools.

title: Barefoot Computing: Primary Computing Resources
description: A UK library of 80+ cross-curricular computing lesson plans for ages 5-11, including an Age 5-7 strand of short, often screen-free activities that teach algorithms, sequencing, and debugging alongside subjects like literacy and PE.
subject: CS / STEM
publisher: Barefoot Computing (BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT)
materials: Varies by lesson; many need no computer
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to describe a sequence of instructions as an algorithm.
Students will be able to spot and fix a mistake (debug) in a simple set of instructions.
price_note: Free with a teacher account registration.
standards: Aligned to the UK National Curriculum for Computing, Key Stage 1 (ages 5-7).
udl_rationale: representation: lessons cross-link computing ideas into literacy/PE so the same concept is met in more than one context; engagement: many activities are physical/unplugged, giving movement-based learners a way in
evidence: over 80 cross-curricular lesson plans and resources that bring computing to life, with or without a computer

title: Climate Change and Cars (K-2 Lesson)
description: A free K-2 lesson from TeachEngineering.org that uses video, guided worksheets, and a think-pair-share discussion to introduce how gas-powered cars affect climate, closing with a formative 'Making Sense' assessment worksheet.
subject: CS / STEM
materials: Printed worksheets; internet access for video; no special equipment
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to explain in simple terms how gas-powered cars contribute to climate change.
Students will be able to complete a 'Making Sense' assessment worksheet showing what they learned about cars and climate.
standards: NGSS-aligned (K-2 Engineering Design / Earth and Human Activity).
udl_rationale: representation: pairs video with a guided worksheet so the same content is delivered by ear and by print; engagement: think-pair-share discussion lets students process the topic verbally with a partner before writing
evidence: Understanding the negative impact gas-powered cars have on the environment empowers engineers to develop alternative modes of transportation.

title: Jack and the Beanstalk: Beanstalk Building
description: A free hands-on K-1 STEM activity from Arizona State University's outreach program where students use simple craft materials to build the tallest possible 'beanstalk,' then measure and compare results with classmates.
subject: CS / STEM
publisher: Arizona STEM Acceleration Project (ASAP), Arizona State University
materials: Simple craft/building materials (e.g., straws, tape, paper) and a measuring tool
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to construct a free-standing tower/structure using basic building materials.
Students will be able to measure their structure's height and compare it with a classmate's using nonstandard or standard units.
source_site: Arizona State University STEM Teachers (ASAP outreach)
udl_rationale: engagement: ties the build challenge to a familiar fairy tale so students have a story hook for the task; action_expression: students show learning by building and measuring a physical object rather than writing about it
evidence: Students build the tallest beanstalk they can with the provided materials. They then measure it and compare their beanstalk heights.

title: TeachEngineering: K-2 STEM Curriculum Search
description: A free, searchable library of NGSS-aligned K-12 STEM lessons and activities from the University of Colorado Boulder; filtering to the K-2 grade band surfaces dozens of vetted, hands-on engineering-design lessons teachers can browse and download.
subject: CS / STEM
publisher: TeachEngineering (University of Colorado Boulder and partner institutions, NSF-funded)
materials: Varies by lesson
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to complete the steps of the engineering design process (ask, imagine, plan, create, improve) in a chosen K-2 lesson.
Students will be able to test a simple prototype and redesign it based on the results.
standards: NGSS Engineering Design; filterable by state and Common Core standards.
udl_rationale: engagement: topic filters (space, robotics, environment, etc.) let teachers match a lesson to what their class is curious about; representation: each lesson bundles video, images, and text so teachers can pick the best format for their students
evidence: Free, standards-aligned STEM curriculum for K-12. A collaboration of the University of Colorado Boulder and partner institutions, funded by the National Science Foundation.

title: 5 African Safari Animals Yoga Poses for Kids
description: Children take an imaginary safari trip and hold five animal yoga poses in sequence: giraffe, zebra, ostrich, elephant, and a cheetah pose where they go onto all fours, extend one leg back and pretend to race. No mat or equipment needed, so it runs on a classroom carpet.
subject: PE / Health
materials: Open floor space; no props required
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to copy and hold five animal-inspired body shapes on cue
Students will be able to name five African safari animals and describe how each one moves
price_note: Pose instructions are free on the page; the site also sells printable yoga cards and books.
udl_rationale: engagement: an imaginary safari journey frames the poses as a story, which sustains attention for children who disengage from drill-style movement; action_expression: children show what they know with their bodies rather than with words, and poses can be simplified or held for shorter counts.
evidence: Pretend to be a racing cheetah.

title: Safari Theme Activities for Pre-K and Preschool
description: A teacher-built safari theme set that includes a two-word brain break: children run in place fast on 'Cheetah!' and freeze or move in slow motion on 'Turtle!'. The rest of the page adds safari art, literacy, math and science ideas built around the same animals.
subject: Science
materials: None for the movement game; other ideas use pattern blocks, cotton balls, cardboard tubes and printables
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to change speed of movement on a spoken cue
Students will be able to match safari animals to how fast or slow they move
price_note: Most ideas are free; some linked printables are sold on Teachers Pay Teachers.
udl_rationale: engagement: a fast/slow contrast game needs no setup and pulls in children who are losing focus mid-lesson; action_expression: the response is whole-body, so children who cannot yet answer verbally still participate fully.
evidence: When you say "Cheetah!", kids run in place super fast.

title: Ocean Animal Movements
description: Printed ocean animal cards are taped around the room, and children travel to each one and act out that animal: opening and closing like a clam, digging like a crab, jumping like a dolphin, singing like a humpback whale. It doubles as a room-scale gross motor circuit.
subject: PE / Health
materials: Free printable ocean animal action cards, cardstock, painter's tape
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to name eight ocean animals
Students will be able to act out a movement that matches each named ocean animal
license: Not stated on page; printable offered as a free download
udl_rationale: engagement: children move around the room instead of sitting, so the activity holds attention far longer than a picture book about the same animals; representation: each animal arrives as a picture, a spoken name and a movement at once, giving three routes to the same vocabulary.
evidence: When you get to a card, point to the picture, say the name of the ocean animal, read the action statement.

title: Move Like a Penguin
description: A movement bank of penguin actions children perform on call: waddling with feet together, flapping wings, sliding on the belly, huddling together for warmth, balancing an 'egg' on the feet, and diving for fish. Runs as Simon Says, a dice roll, or a card draw.
subject: PE / Health
materials: None required; optional movement cards or a large foam dice
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to balance on one foot and walk with feet together in a penguin waddle
Students will be able to describe two ways real penguins move in their icy habitat
udl_rationale: engagement: the teacher can pick two moves for a 60-second wiggle break or run the whole set as a lesson, matching the class's energy; action_expression: several moves target different skills (balancing, sliding, hopping), so a child who cannot hop can still slide or huddle.
evidence: Encourage children to get creative with their movements and have fun exploring the various ways penguins navigate their icy habitats!

title: Dinosaur Roll and Move Gross Motor Activity
description: Children take turns rolling a soft pocket cube loaded with dinosaur movement cards, then the whole group performs whatever came up — twisting like a T-Rex, stretching tall like a Brachiosaurus. Turn-taking around the cube is built into the game.
subject: PE / Health
materials: Soft pocket cube, free printable dinosaur movement cards, scissors, optional laminator
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to perform a movement that matches the dinosaur shown on the card
Students will be able to wait for their turn to roll the cube
udl_rationale: engagement: the random roll keeps the next move unknown, which sustains interest through repeated rounds; action_expression: children respond with large body movements and each card can be scaled down for a child with limited mobility.
evidence: Waiting for a turn is a very difficult for young children which helps them develop self-regulation skills.

title: Act Out the Life Cycle of a Butterfly
description: A no-materials creative movement sequence: children curl into balls as eggs, wiggle along the floor as hungry caterpillars, stand still with arms wrapped as a chrysalis, then spread their arms and fly as butterflies. The teacher narrates each stage as a cue.
subject: Science
materials: None; optional picture books about butterflies
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to act out the four stages of the butterfly life cycle in order
Students will be able to name the egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly stages
udl_rationale: engagement: acting out metamorphosis turns an abstract sequence into something children feel in their own bodies, which holds three-year-olds far better than a diagram; action_expression: sequence knowledge is demonstrated through movement, so pre-readers and children with limited expressive language can show mastery.
evidence: Start out as tiny eggs, rolled up in a ball on the floor!

title: Caterpillar and Butterfly Life Cycle Art Activity: Shape Caterpillars
description: Children glue pre-cut circles and rectangles onto green paper to build a caterpillar body, feet and antennae, then add details with markers. The finished caterpillars become pages in a small life cycle book covering egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly.
subject: Science
materials: Green construction paper, pre-cut circles and rectangles, squeeze-bottle glue, markers, crayons, binder rings
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to build a caterpillar using circle and rectangle shapes
Students will be able to order the four stages of the butterfly life cycle in a book
udl_rationale: representation: the life cycle is presented as a sequence of physical pages the child can turn and revisit, not a one-time verbal explanation; action_expression: children build and draw rather than write, and the pre-cut shapes remove the scissor barrier for children still developing hand strength.
evidence: Using glue from a squeeze bottle requires effort, which is a great way to sneak in some hand/arm strengthening!

title: Farm Animals - Music & Movement Lesson Plan
description: A full circle-time music session built on farm animals: a hello song with actions, parachute play, animal sound call-and-response, the Chicken Dance, high and low pitch with instruments, and acting out each animal to music before a goodbye song.
subject: Arts
materials: Parachute, music player, farm animal pictures, beach ball, percussion instruments (tambourines, shakers, bells)
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to make the sound and movement that matches each farm animal
Students will be able to tell the difference between a high and a low pitch
udl_rationale: engagement: the session cycles through parachute, singing, instruments and dance, so a child who tunes out of one format is re-engaged by the next within minutes; representation: each farm animal is delivered as a picture, a sound, a song lyric and a movement.
evidence: How fun it is to visit the farm! Don't you love farm animals?

title: From Seeds to Plants
description: A short PreK science lesson where the teacher shows a live plant and a handful of seeds, then leads children through what a seed needs - soil, water, sunshine - before they observe and discuss how a seed becomes a plant.
subject: Science
materials: Live plant, seeds, soil, water, sunlight
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to identify how seeds develop into plants
Students will be able to name what a seed needs in order to grow
price_note: The lesson text is readable free; Education.com also sells a premium membership for some downloads.
udl_rationale: representation: children handle real seeds and a real plant alongside the spoken explanation, which anchors an abstract process in something concrete; engagement: the lesson connects to a planting project children can tend over following days, giving the learning a visible payoff.
evidence: Tell students that today they will be learning how seeds grow and develop into plants with the help of soil, water, sunshine, and carbon dioxide.

title: Autumn Leaves Preschool Science
description: Children collect red and yellow autumn leaves, then press half of them under heavy books overnight and leave the rest in the open air. Over three days they compare the two groups by look, feel and smell, and record what changed.
subject: Science
materials: Fresh autumn leaves, heavy books, white paper, free printable observation chart
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to describe how a leaf changes over three days
Students will be able to compare two groups of leaves by texture and colour
license: Not stated on page; observation chart offered as a free download
udl_rationale: representation: children gather evidence through sight, touch and smell rather than through a single verbal explanation of what leaves do in autumn; engagement: the outdoor collection walk and the multi-day wait give children a stake in the result.
evidence: The crunch of dried leaves, the weight of heavy books, and the interesting results of the experiment all stack up to make this a fun fall activity.

title: Rain Cloud in a Jar
description: A four-step weather demonstration children run themselves: fill a clear jar with water, spray shaving cream on top for the cloud, then drip food colouring onto the foam and watch the colour sink through in streaks like falling rain.
subject: Science
materials: Clear glass jar, water, white shaving cream, liquid food colouring, dropper
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to explain that rain falls when a cloud holds too much water
Students will be able to predict and then describe what happens to the colour in the jar
udl_rationale: representation: an invisible process in the sky becomes a visible one in a jar, at the child's eye level; engagement: the dropper work gives every child a turn at the moment the rain appears, rather than watching the teacher demonstrate.
evidence: The food coloring is sinking through the shaving cream cloud, like real rain falls from the sky!

title: Geometry for Kids: Finding Shapes at the Playground
description: Children take a printable shape checklist out to the playground and hunt for circles, squares, rectangles and triangles in the climbing frames and equipment, photographing each find. The photos are then printed and stapled into a labelled shape book.
subject: Math
materials: Free printable shape hunt checklist, camera or phone, printer, paper, stapler
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to find and name circles, squares, rectangles and triangles in the real world
Students will be able to match a found object to the shape word on a checklist
udl_rationale: engagement: shape learning moves outdoors onto equipment children already love, which reaches learners who disengage from worksheet geometry; action_expression: children demonstrate shape knowledge by pointing, photographing and building a book instead of by writing.
evidence: As we walked around the playground we found circles, squares, rectangles, and triangles from different angles in the play structures.

title: Five Little Ducks Number Line Gross Motor Activity
description: Numbered duck cards are taped to the floor in order to make a walkable number line. Children hop, jump or step from duck to duck saying each number aloud. Numbers can be swapped out of order, or one removed, for children to spot what is missing.
subject: Math
materials: Free printable duck number cards, tape, optional laminator
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to count aloud from one to five while stepping along a number line
Students will be able to identify a missing number in a sequence
price_note: The printable is delivered through a free email sign-up.
udl_rationale: engagement: pairing counting with a familiar song and with hopping keeps children in the activity longer than counters at a table; action_expression: a child shows number order by moving their body along the line, which works before they can write numerals.
evidence: Counting is an important early math skill that's a precursor to learning number names and values.

title: ABC Cookies Preschool Alphabet Activity
description: A bakery dramatic play set-up for letter matching: paper plates are labelled with lowercase letters, and children lift foam uppercase letters with a spatula onto the matching plate, then serve the 'cookies' to dolls or classmates.
subject: ELA / Reading
materials: Small paper plates labelled with lowercase letters, foam alphabet letters, baking sheet, spatula, optional apron
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to match an uppercase letter to its lowercase partner
Students will be able to name the letters they serve during play
udl_rationale: engagement: embedding letter matching inside a bakery role-play gives a purpose children care about, unlike flashcard drill; action_expression: children handle, scoop and serve physical letters, so success does not depend on naming letters aloud.
evidence: Tinker loved matching the upper and lowercase letters as she served up a whole batch of ABC cookies.

title: A is for Apple: Building Letter-Recognition Fluency
description: Children hunt for hidden letter cards around the room, visit online alphabet games to find words starting with each letter, then draw a picture for every letter to build their own ABC book, which they read to a partner.
subject: ELA / Reading
materials: Hidden letter cards on cardstock, chart paper, index cards, computers with internet access, My ABC Book handout
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to recognise and name letters of the alphabet fluently
Students will be able to produce a word beginning with a given letter and illustrate it
standards: Common Core State Standards; NCTE/IRA National Standards for the English Language Arts
udl_rationale: representation: letters are met as physical cards, as online game targets and as drawings, so the same content reaches children through three channels; action_expression: children show mastery by searching, drawing and reading aloud rather than only by writing.
evidence: Becoming fluent in letter recognition helps children to become more familiar and at ease with the alphabet.

title: Calm Down Corner Printables and Ideas
description: A guide to setting up one quiet classroom corner with soft seating, a sensory bottle and free printable strategy cards, plus an 'I Can Calm Down' book children page through to pick a strategy such as deep breathing when they feel upset.
subject: SEL
materials: Free printable calm down strategy cards, 'I Can Calm Down' book, emotion picture-word cards, cushion or bean bag, sensory bottle
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to choose a calming strategy from the picture cards
Students will be able to name the feeling they are having using the emotion cards
price_note: Printables are free; the site also sells related packs on Teachers Pay Teachers.
license: Printables are for personal, non-commercial use only
udl_rationale: engagement: children choose their own strategy and their own timing, which builds self-regulation rather than relying on adult direction; representation: strategies appear as pictures plus words, so a pre-reader can use the cards independently.
evidence: Young children are still learning how to manage their emotions

title: Emotions Activity with Paper Plate Faces
description: Children paint paper plates as faces, then use velcro-backed eye and mouth shapes to swap expressions on and off. A named feeling or a short scenario is called out and children build the face that matches it.
subject: SEL
materials: Paper plates, acrylic paint and brushes, foam sheets or felt, velcro dots, popsicle sticks
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to build a face that matches a named feeling
Students will be able to name at least four feelings from their facial expressions
udl_rationale: representation: feelings are shown as changeable physical features rather than described in words, which makes the link between expression and emotion concrete; action_expression: a child answers by moving velcro pieces, so children with little expressive language can still show they understand.
evidence: Being aware of feelings and why they get them, can help them learn how to control their reactions to strong emotions in the future.

title: Chinese Dragon for the New Year
description: The class builds a wearable dragon head from a painted cardboard box with egg-carton eyes and yarn, then a line of children carries a blanket behind it as the body and parades through the school while classmates play instruments alongside.
subject: Social Studies
materials: Large cardboard box, paint and brushes, egg carton, yarn, glue, string, jewels, blanket, classroom instruments
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to explain what the dragon stands for in Lunar New Year celebrations
Students will be able to move together as one group to carry the dragon in a parade
price_note: The activity page is free; the source book is sold separately.
udl_rationale: engagement: a whole-class parade gives every child a visible role and ties a cultural celebration to something they build themselves; action_expression: children can take part by constructing, by carrying the dragon, or by playing an instrument, so there are three ways in.
evidence: The Chinese dragon is a symbol of strength, wisdom, health, and good luck.

title: We're Going on a Bear Hunt Early Years Activities
description: Eight classroom activities built on the story, including 'Mission Impossible: Bear Hunt', where children run an outdoor obstacle course and copy each movement as the teacher narrates - wading through long grass, trudging through mud, tiptoeing into the cave.
subject: ELA / Reading
materials: Outdoor or indoor space, cushions, fabric, sensory trays with water, mud, sand and grass; the picture book
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to retell the story in order by moving through matching obstacles
Students will be able to use positional words such as over, under and through
udl_rationale: engagement: the obstacle course makes story sequence something children move through rather than sit and listen to, which suits children who cannot hold still for a full read-aloud; action_expression: retelling is demonstrated physically, so children who are not yet talking in full sentences can still show they know the order.
evidence: Encourage the children to imitate their movements as you read the story aloud.

title: Moon Phases with Cookies
description: Students scrape the frosting inside Oreo-style sandwich cookies to sculpt each of the eight moon phases, then line the cookies up in order to model one full lunar cycle.
subject: Science
materials: 8 sandwich cookies per student or pair, popsicle stick or plastic scraper
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to name and sequence the eight phases of the moon
Students will be able to explain that moon phases come from how much sunlit moon we can see from Earth
udl_rationale: engagement: food and sculpting make an abstract sky pattern immediately appealing; representation: the frosting gives a concrete visual of an otherwise distant phenomenon; action_expression: students show understanding by shaping and ordering models rather than writing definitions
evidence: Use the popsicle stick or scraper to create the phases of the moon out of the frosting.

title: Moon Phases (Act Out the Lunar Cycle)
description: Each student holds a Styrofoam ball on a pencil and turns slowly in place around a bright lamp, becoming Earth while the ball becomes the moon, watching all eight phases appear on their own model.
subject: Science
materials: One white Styrofoam ball (5 cm or larger) and pencil per student, one bright incandescent lamp (100W+)
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to model the relative positions of the sun, Earth and moon
Students will be able to predict which moon phase is visible from a given sun-Earth-moon arrangement
udl_rationale: engagement: whole-body role play keeps every student physically involved; representation: the lamp-and-sphere model converts a 3D spatial relationship into something students can see directly; action_expression: understanding is demonstrated by positioning the model, not by verbal recall
evidence: Explain to students that the bulb is the sun, each of their spheres is the moon and each student is Earth

title: Solar System Bead Activity
description: Students thread colored pony beads onto a 5-metre string at measured distances to build a wearable scale model of the solar system, where the spacing itself does the teaching.
subject: Math
materials: Colored craft pony beads, 5 m of string per student, cardboard holder, meter sticks or rulers, student worksheet
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to measure and place objects at scaled distances along a number line
Students will be able to describe how much farther apart the outer planets are than the inner planets
udl_rationale: representation: distance data becomes a physical object students can hold and compare; action_expression: students demonstrate scale reasoning by measuring and building, with calculation optional for students ready for it
evidence: Students construct -- and where appropriate, calculate -- a scale model of the solar system using beads and string.

title: Create a Comet with Dry Ice
description: The teacher mixes crushed dry ice with water, dirt, starch and syrup to build a real, steaming model comet in front of the class, then shines a flashlight on it to show how sunlight drives a tail.
subject: Science
materials: Dry ice, insulated container, thick gloves and goggles, mallet, large bowl, water, dirt, starch, corn syrup, flat tray, flashlight, hairdryer, data sheet
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to describe what a comet is made of
Students will be able to observe and record a change of state from solid to gas
udl_rationale: engagement: a smoking, hissing comet on the front desk is a genuine spectacle that anchors attention; representation: an object millions of kilometres away becomes a tangible thing students can watch change
evidence: Comets are cosmic snowballs of frozen gases, rock and dust, roughly the size of a small town.

title: Mars Rover Driver Board Game
description: Teams take the roles of scientist, engineer and rover driver, writing sequences of arrow commands to steer a rover across a printed Mars board under power and cargo limits.
subject: CS / STEM
materials: Printable game board and worksheet (PDF), colored marbles or small rocks, a toy rover or car, tape
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to write an ordered sequence of commands to move a rover to a target
Students will be able to justify a choice of samples under power and mass constraints
udl_rationale: engagement: a competitive game with real mission roles gives a clear goal and social buy-in; action_expression: students express programming logic through physical moves and symbol sequences instead of typed code
evidence: Students learn to write basic command sequences, which lay the groundwork for developing computer programming skills.

title: Art and the Cosmic Connection
description: Students study real NASA images of planets, moons and asteroids for line, shape, colour and texture, then recreate a chosen surface in soft pastel and explain the geology they drew.
subject: Arts
materials: Drawing paper (9x12 in or larger), soft pastels, gummy erasers, Q-tips, wipes, downloadable slide deck and reference images
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to identify shape, line, colour, texture and value in a planetary image
Students will be able to describe a surface feature of a solar system object in their own artwork
udl_rationale: engagement: students choose which world to draw, which gives real ownership; representation: scientific content arrives visually rather than through text; action_expression: artwork plus spoken reflection lets non-writers show what they learned
evidence: Utilizing art-making as a vehicle for scientific inquiry inspires and engages students, preparing them for a more rigorous exploration of space science.

title: Planetary Poetry
description: Students pick a NASA mission or space image, fill in a KWL chart about it, learn one poetic form, then write a poem about their chosen world using accurate details.
subject: ELA / Reading
materials: Example poems (PDF), paper and pencils, access to NASA mission images and videos
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to gather facts about a space topic and record them on a KWL chart
Students will be able to write an original poem in a taught form using accurate topic details
udl_rationale: engagement: students choose their own space topic, so the writing has a subject they already care about; action_expression: several poetic forms are offered, so students can pick a structure that fits their writing confidence
evidence: Space has been a source of inspiration and the subject of creative endeavors for ages.

title: Ready to Erupt! Model Volcano Measurement
description: The class builds a sand volcano over a water balloon and hose, then fills the balloon so the mountain visibly swells before it erupts, measuring the height at each stage like real volcanologists.
subject: Science
materials: 30-50 lbs sand, water balloon with filler and valve, garden hose, wooden board, cinder blocks, metal can, ruler, worksheet
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to name the main parts of a volcano
Students will be able to explain how a rising magma chamber warns engineers of an eruption
price_note: Free to access; the demonstration needs low-cost materials such as sand and a garden hose
license: Copyright 2006 by Regents of the University of Colorado
udl_rationale: engagement: an actual eruption in the classroom creates strong anticipation; representation: an invisible underground process is made visible at classroom scale; action_expression: students record learning through measurements and sketches as well as written answers
evidence: Engineers design and build devices to detect indications of an impending eruption.

title: Strawkets and Thrust
description: Students roll two paper rockets around pencils of different widths, then launch each by blowing through a straw at a planet target, comparing flights to see how nozzle size changes thrust.
subject: Science
materials: Half sheets of paper, pencil, drinking straw, cotton ball and tape per student; planet target pictures
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to describe thrust and name one factor that changes it
Students will be able to compare the flight of two rockets and explain the difference
price_note: Free to access; uses paper, straws and tape
license: Copyright 2006 by Regents of the University of Colorado
udl_rationale: engagement: launching a rocket the student built themselves is an immediate hook with a visible result; action_expression: students show what they understand by building, launching and comparing flights rather than by explaining a formula
evidence: The nozzle size and shape effects how fast the exhaust leaves the rocket as well as how much pressure it will have.

title: Reverse Engineering: Ball Bounce Experiment
description: Groups drop four different sports balls from set heights, measure how high each bounces and time how long it keeps bouncing, then chart results and work out why each ball is built the way it is.
subject: Math
materials: Four different balls (e.g. basketball, tennis, golf, rubber), stopwatch and yardstick per group, worksheets
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to collect and record measurement data from repeated trials
Students will be able to build and interpret a graph comparing how different balls bounce
price_note: Free to access; uses balls and rulers a school already has

title: Testing Model Structures: Jell-O Earthquake in the Classroom

udl_rationale: engagement: shaking a tower until it falls is a fast, memorable failure students want to fix; action_expression: the redesign-and-retest cycle lets students demonstrate reasoning through building rather than writing
evidence: Cross-bracing supports and balances tension and compression forces to help prevent the structure from collapsing during an earthquake.

title: Save the Bats

udl_rationale: engagement: a blindfolded game turns an abstract sense into a game students want to play; representation: story, diagrams, photographs and a physical skull present the same content four ways; action_expression: students respond through movement and discussion, not worksheets
evidence: Students will learn how they can help protect bats against human intervention and natural threats such as White-Nose Syndrome.

title: A Fossil's Journey
description: Three short hands-on rounds: students press shells and leaves into layered mud to make body fossils, carve tracks into clay for trace fossils, then sort which parts of an animal fossilise at all.
subject: Science

udl_rationale: engagement: making and breaking your own fossils taps directly into the dinosaur interest most of this age group already has; representation: the same idea is met through moulding, carving and diagram analysis; action_expression: students show understanding through physical models before the written post-assessment
evidence: Fossils need not be mineralized (turned to rock) or even enclosed in rock.

title: How Do Hurricanes Form? (NOAA SciJinks)

title: All About Me: All of Me
subject: SEL
description: Preschool day plan from the 'All About Me' thematic week (September): All of Me. Focus book: Me and My Amazing Body — Joan Sweeney. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Me and My Amazing Body — Joan Sweeney

Language Arts — Goal: Name body parts and say what each part does.
Activity: We will read the focus book at circle time, pointing to and naming each body part as it appears. Children will then place picture labels on a large body-outline poster and tell a partner one thing that part helps them do.
Materials: Focus book; body-outline poster; body-part picture labels
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Picture labels a child can place and point to instead of naming aloud, for emerging talkers.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Use a mirror to observe my own features.
Activity: Children will look into hand mirrors at the science table and describe what they see — eye color, hair, a smile. We will compare observations with a friend and notice that we each look a little different.
Materials: Hand mirrors; observation paper; crayons
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: A larger mirror on a stand and extra looking time for children who need longer to observe and describe.

Social Science — Goal: Share one fact about myself with the class.
Activity: Each child will complete the sentence frame 'My name is... and I am ... years old' using a name card, and share it with the group. The teacher will chart our names so we can see our whole class together.
Materials: Name cards; sentence-frame cards; chart paper
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Children may hold up their name card and let the teacher say the frame with them.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count body parts that come in pairs and in tens.
Activity: We will count eyes, ears, arms, and hands in pairs, then count all ten fingers while wiggling them. Children will match number cards to the groups we counted on a felt face.
Materials: Felt face pieces; number cards 1–10
Grouping: Small group — math center; teacher-guided
Support: Touch-and-count with hand-over-hand support and a number strip as a visual anchor.

Creative Art — Goal: Trace and decorate a life-size outline of my body.
Activity: Partners will lie on butcher paper while the teacher traces each child's outline. Children will color in clothes and features to make the outline look like themselves.
Materials: Butcher paper; crayons; markers
Grouping: Small groups — art area; teacher-assisted
Support: A smaller paper option and chunky crayons for children who are not comfortable being traced.

Music / Movement — Goal: Follow directions to move named body parts in a song.
Activity: We will sing the head-shoulders-knees-and-toes song slowly, touching each part on cue, then sing it faster and see if our hands can keep up.
Materials: Recorded song; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A seated version and body-part picture cards held up as cues for children who need them.

Motor Activities — Goal: Strengthen fingers by rolling and pinching playdough.
Activity: Children will roll, pinch, and press playdough to build a little person — a round head, a body, arms, and legs — on their mats.
Materials: Playdough; mats; small rolling pins
Grouping: Centers — fine motor table; child-led
Support: Softer dough and dough tools (rollers, cutters) for children building hand strength.

Technology — Goal: Take a self-portrait photo with the class camera.
Activity: With the teacher, each child will take a photo of themselves smiling at the camera corner. We will view the photos together on the screen and name our friends.
Materials: Class tablet on a stand (teacher-managed); projector
Grouping: Small groups — classroom corner; teacher-led
Support: The teacher holds and aims the tablet while the child presses the button, for children still learning device care.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Use my whole body to run, jump, and balance.
Activity: Outside, children will follow a movement path: jump over chalk lines, walk the low balance beam, and toss beanbags into a hoop.
Materials: Chalk lines; low balance beam; beanbags; hoop
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-supervised
Support: A shorter path and a partner to walk the beam with, for children who need support.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn that my body is special and worth taking care of.
Activity: We will talk about ways we care for our bodies — washing hands, resting, eating good food, and moving. Each child will name or point to one caring thing they do.
Materials: Body-care picture cards; chart paper
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Picture cards to choose from for children who cannot yet think of an answer to say.

title: All About Me: Moving Like the Animals
subject: SEL
description: Preschool day plan from the 'All About Me' thematic week (September): Moving Like the Animals. Focus book: From Head to Toe — Eric Carle. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: From Head to Toe — Eric Carle

Language Arts — Goal: Retell a story by acting out its sequence of movements.
Activity: We will read the focus book and do each animal's movement as the pages turn — bending, wiggling, and stomping along. Afterwards children will put the animal cards in the order they appeared in the book.
Materials: Focus book; animal movement cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Movement cards shown as a cue before each page, and a seated option for every movement.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Observe how animals move and compare their bodies to ours.
Activity: Children will look closely at animal photos, try each animal's movement, and notice which of our body parts bend like the animal's. We will share one movement our bodies can do and one only the animal can.
Materials: Animal photos; hand mirrors
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Extra time to try each movement, with the teacher modeling slowly beside the child.

Social Science — Goal: Take turns being the movement leader.
Activity: One child at a time will pick a movement card and lead the class in copying it. We will practice watching our leader and waiting for our turn to lead.
Materials: Movement card basket; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Choosing a card to lead from, instead of inventing a movement, for children who feel unsure.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Sort pictures by the number of legs: two, four, or none.
Activity: Children will sort animal cards into three hoops by counting legs, then count how many animals landed in each hoop and say which group has the most.
Materials: Animal picture cards; sorting hoops; counting cubes
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: Start with just two hoops (two legs / four legs) for children building sorting stamina.

Creative Art — Goal: Make prints with my hands and feet.
Activity: Children will press painted handprints and footprints onto paper to make animals and flowers — a handprint can become an elephant, a footprint a carrot top. We will wash up carefully with wipes and at the sink.
Materials: Washable tempera paint; large paper; smocks; wipes
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A sponge-brush print option for children who dislike paint on their skin.

Music / Movement — Goal: Sing a body song at different speeds.
Activity: We will sing our body-parts song in slow motion like a turtle, then at regular speed, then zippy-fast, noticing how our breathing and muscles feel each time.
Materials: Teacher-led singing; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Visual speed cards (turtle, walker, rabbit) so children can anticipate each tempo change.

Motor Activities — Goal: Copy and hold animal poses to build balance and core strength.
Activity: Children will draw pose cards (flamingo stand, bear crawl, frog squat) and hold each pose while the class counts to five together.
Materials: Pose cards; mats
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A wall within reach for balance support and a shorter count for children who are practicing.

Technology — Goal: Hear my own voice naming body parts on a recording.
Activity: Children will record themselves saying one sentence — 'My elbows bend' — into the class voice recorder. We will play the recordings back and guess whose voice we hear.
Materials: Voice recorder or tablet with recording app
Grouping: Small group — quiet corner; teacher-guided
Support: Recording with a partner saying it together, for children who are shy about their voice alone.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Play follow-the-leader with body movements outdoors.
Activity: On the playground path, the leader of the line will choose a movement — marching, tiptoeing, swinging arms — and everyone behind copies until the next leader's turn.
Materials: Playground path; open space
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A buddy partner walking alongside for children who need help staying with the line.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn that every body moves in its own way, and that is okay.
Activity: We will talk about how bodies move differently — some friends run fast, some use wheels or walkers to get around — and every way of moving is good. Each child will share a movement their body loves to do.
Materials: Focus book (favorite pages); feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Specific praise naming what each child shared, so every contribution is valued out loud.

Focus book: My Five Senses — Aliki

Language Arts — Goal: Use sense words in sentences: I see, I hear, I smell, I touch.
Activity: After reading the focus book, we will add sense words with icons to our word wall. Children will finish sentence strips — 'I hear with my ears' — and read them to a partner.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Use listening to identify mystery sounds.
Activity: Children will shake sealed shakers filled with rice, beans, and bells, listen carefully, and guess what is inside. We will open one together to check our best guess and chart how we did.

Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Two picture choices to point to for each guess, for children who need language support.

Social Science — Goal: Work with a partner to complete a senses hunt.
Activity: Partners will carry a picture checklist around our classroom stations to find something rough, something smooth, something that makes a sound, and something colorful. Partners will check off each find together.
Materials: Picture checklists on clipboards; pencils; station materials
Grouping: Pairs — around the classroom; child-led
Support: Partner pairing with a confident reader of the picture checklist, and a shorter list (three items).

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Make a graph of our favorite sense to explore.
Activity: Each child will place their name card in a graph column for the sense station they enjoyed most today. We will count each column and say which sense was our class favorite.
Materials: Pocket-chart graph; name cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Counting each column aloud with a partner, pointing to every card.

Creative Art — Goal: Create touch art with many textures.
Activity: Children will glue fabric scraps, sandpaper, cotton balls, and foil onto card stock to make a touch picture, then describe how each part feels with their eyes closed.
Materials: Texture scraps; card stock; glue sticks
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A glue sponge and pre-cut texture pieces for children building cutting and squeezing skills.

Music / Movement — Goal: Identify instruments by sound alone.
Activity: The teacher will play instruments hidden behind a small screen — drum, shaker, bell, guiro — and children will name or point to what they hear. Then everyone gets a turn to play and be guessed.
Materials: Rhythm instruments; small screen; instrument picture cards
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Instrument picture cards to point to, and a volume check so no sound startles anyone.

Motor Activities — Goal: Use tongs and pincer grasp to sort pom-poms by color.
Activity: Children will move pom-poms with tongs into matching cups of a muffin tin, working slowly to keep their grip. We will count how many pom-poms fit in each cup at the end.
Materials: Tongs; pom-poms; muffin tins; color cups
Grouping: Centers — fine motor table
Support: Easy-squeeze tongs and larger pom-poms for children developing grip strength.

Technology — Goal: Look very closely with a digital microscope.
Activity: With the teacher, small groups will use the digital microscope to examine a leaf, a piece of fabric, and the back of a hand, watching the magnified view on the screen and describing the tiny details.
Materials: Digital microscope; screen; leaf and fabric samples
Grouping: Small groups — science table; teacher-led
Support: Adult proximity and a turn-taking timer so every child gets a calm, unhurried look.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Use my senses on a quiet outdoor minute.
Activity: Outside, we will sit on sit-spots for one quiet minute — listening, looking, and smelling the air — then share one thing each sense noticed. Each child will collect one fallen leaf to bring to the science table.
Materials: Sit spots; leaf collection bag
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A defined sit spot close to the teacher and a buddy to share observations with first.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn that pausing to notice my senses can help me feel calm.
Activity: We will practice 'smell the flower, blow out the candle' breathing, using our fingers as the flower and the candle. Children will share when this breathing might help them during the day.
Materials: Breathing prompt card; quiet corner
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: One-on-one practice with the teacher first, for children who need the steps modeled closely.

title: All About Me: What I Look Like
subject: SEL
description: Preschool day plan from the 'All About Me' thematic week (September): What I Look Like. Focus book: It's Okay to Be Different — Todd Parr. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: It's Okay to Be Different — Todd Parr

Language Arts — Goal: Describe my own appearance with describing words.
Activity: After reading the focus book, children will look in mirrors and dictate a page for our class book: 'I have brown hair and brown eyes. I wear glasses.' The teacher will write each child's words under their drawing.
Materials: Focus book; mirrors; class book pages; crayons
Grouping: Large group then independent — carpet/tables
Support: A word bank with pictures (hair colors, curly/straight, glasses) to point to while dictating.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Observe and compare colors in our hair, eyes, and skin.
Activity: Children will sort yarn and fabric samples in many shades, find samples close to their own hair color, and lay them in a row from lightest to darkest. We will notice how many shades our class has.
Materials: Yarn and fabric samples in many shades; sorting trays
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Fewer samples per round (start with five) for children who are building comparison skills.

Social Science — Goal: Play a game that shows we can be the same and different at once.
Activity: We will play 'Stand If You...' — stand if you have curly hair, stand if you have brown eyes, stand if you like pizza. Children will see the groups change every time: different in some ways, the same in others.
Materials: Open rug space; teacher prompt cards
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: The teacher reads each cue slowly twice, and children may move with a buddy.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Measure and compare heights.
Activity: Children will stand against our height chart to mark their height with tape, then build a cube tower the same number of cubes as their paper height strip. We will compare towers using taller and shorter.
Materials: Height chart; tape; paper strips; cubes
Grouping: Small groups — math center; teacher-assisted
Support: A partner to hold the strip steady, and taller/shorter picture cards as vocabulary support.

Creative Art — Goal: Draw a self-portrait that looks like me.
Activity: Looking in mirrors, children will draw their own faces, choosing crayons and skin-tone colors that match themselves, and glue on yarn hair in their own style.
Materials: Mirrors; crayons including skin-tone sets; yarn; glue
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A face-outline template available for children who want a starting shape, and chunky crayons.

Music / Movement — Goal: Sing a song that celebrates our differences.
Activity: We will learn a simple teacher-led song about how our class has many colors of hair, eyes, and skin, and nobody looks exactly the same. Children will point to their own hair and eyes at the matching verses.
Materials: Teacher-led song; mirror prop
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Action cues (point to hair, point to eyes) demonstrated by the teacher throughout.

Motor Activities — Goal: Build playdough faces with features I choose.
Activity: Children will flatten playdough into a face shape and press in features — bead eyes, yarn hair, a dough smile — making the face look any way they like.
Materials: Playdough; large beads; yarn pieces; mats
Grouping: Centers — fine motor table
Support: Dough tools for pressing features and larger beads for children who need an easier grasp.

Technology — Goal: View our class slideshow and name my classmates.
Activity: The teacher will project photos from our theme so far — portraits, families, and work — and children will call out the name of each friend they see. We will count how many friends are in our class family.
Materials: Projector; class photos from the theme
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Front-row seating for children who need to see the screen up close.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Hunt for colors outdoors that match me.
Activity: Children will carry two paint-chip cards chosen to match their hair, eyes, or clothes, and hunt outside for leaves, flowers, or stones of the same colors.
Materials: Paint-chip cards; clipboards
Grouping: Pairs — outdoors; teacher-supervised
Support: Just two colors to find, and a partner to hunt with, for children who need a smaller task.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn that different is interesting, and kind words celebrate it.
Activity: We will practice giving a partner a compliment about something we can see — 'I like your curly hair' or 'Your smile is friendly.' The teacher will model one first and celebrate each compliment given.
Materials: Compliment sentence-frame card
Grouping: Pairs — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A sentence frame and picture compliment cards for children who need help finding the words.

title: All About Me: My Hands and Feet Can Do
subject: SEL
description: Preschool day plan from the 'All About Me' thematic week (September): My Hands and Feet Can Do. Focus book: Wonderful Hands — — a picture book celebrating all the things hands can do (substitute any hands-and-feet title on hand). Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Wonderful Hands — — a picture book celebrating all the things hands can do (substitute any hands-and-feet title on hand)

Language Arts — Goal: Name action words for things hands can do.
Activity: After reading the focus book, we will brainstorm action words — clap, wave, build, hug, draw — and act out each one as the teacher adds it to our action-word chart.
Materials: Focus book; action-word chart; markers
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Action picture cards children can act out instead of naming, for emerging talkers.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Investigate fingerprints and discover that everyone's are unique.
Activity: Children will press a thumb onto a washable ink pad, stamp their print on paper, and study it with a magnifier. We will compare prints side by side and notice that no two look the same.
Materials: Washable ink pads; paper; magnifiers; wipes
Grouping: Small groups — science table; teacher-supervised
Support: A sponge ink pad for an easier press, and hand-over-hand guidance for children who need it.

Social Science — Goal: Choose a helping-hands job for the day.
Activity: We will look at our job chart and talk about how hands help our classroom — line leader, plant waterer, table wiper. Each child will choose or be given a helping job and practice it once with the teacher.
Materials: Picture job chart; classroom job props
Grouping: Large group then independent; teacher-guided
Support: Jobs shown as pictures, with a partner-job option for children who want to work alongside a friend.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Measure with my hand span and count my fingers.
Activity: Children will trace their hands, count all the fingers, then measure the art table in hand spans and record the number. We will compare hand-span counts and talk about why they differ.
Materials: Paper; crayons; recording sheet
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: A pre-traced hand outline for children who find tracing hard, and counting support from the teacher.

Creative Art — Goal: Make a handprint keepsake picture.
Activity: Children will paint one hand and press it onto card stock to make a handprint flower or animal, adding fingerprint details. Names and dates go on the back for our portfolios.
Materials: Washable paint; card stock; smocks; wipes
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Paint applied with a brush to the hand instead of dipping, for children sensitive to the feeling of paint.

Music / Movement — Goal: Copy clapping patterns with my hands.
Activity: The teacher will clap short patterns — clap, clap, pause, clap — and children will echo them. Volunteers will lead their own pattern for the class to copy.
Materials: Open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Pattern cards showing hand icons, and the option to pat knees instead of clapping.

Motor Activities — Goal: Build finger strength with clothespins and lacing.
Activity: Children will clip clothespins around the edge of a paper plate 'sun,' then lace a hand-shaped card with a thick lace, in and out of every hole.
Materials: Clothespins; paper plates; hand lacing cards; thick laces
Grouping: Centers — fine motor table
Support: Easy-spring clothespins and a lace with a stiffened tip for children building pinch strength.

Technology — Goal: Explore light and shadow with hand shapes.
Activity: At the light table, children will make hand shadows and shapes, trace around their hand's shadow on translucent paper, and compare big and small shadows by moving closer and farther.
Materials: Light table; translucent paper; pencils
Grouping: Small groups — science/light area; teacher-guided
Support: A partner to hold the paper steady while the child traces.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Follow a footprint path with my feet.
Activity: Outside, children will follow chalk footprints on the pavement: tiptoe steps, stomps, hops, and giant steps, changing how their feet move at each section.
Materials: Chalk footprint path; open pavement
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-supervised
Support: A wider path and the choice to walk the hopping sections, for children still building jumping skills.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn that gentle hands are kind hands.
Activity: We will practice gentle touches by stroking a stuffed animal softly and passing it carefully around our circle. Then we will add our handprints to a class pledge poster: 'My hands are for helping and being gentle.'
Materials: Stuffed animal; pledge poster; paint for handprints
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Modeling right beside the child and specific praise each time gentle hands are used.

title: All About Me: Feelings on My Face
subject: SEL
description: Preschool day plan from the 'All About Me' thematic week (September): Feelings on My Face. Focus book: The Feelings Book — Todd Parr. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: The Feelings Book — Todd Parr

Language Arts — Goal: Name feeling words: happy, sad, mad, scared, silly.
Activity: We will read the focus book and make each feeling face as it appears. Children will match feelings face cards to the words on our chart and show the face that matches.
Materials: Focus book; feelings face cards; feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A small mirror to copy each face, and pointing to match instead of naming for emerging talkers.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Observe how faces change when feelings change.
Activity: Children will sort photo cards of children's expressions into feeling groups, looking closely at eyebrows, eyes, and mouths to decide. We will talk about the clues faces give us.
Materials: Expression photo cards; sorting mats
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Only two feelings to sort at a time (happy/sad) before adding more choices.

Social Science — Goal: Notice a friend's feelings and respond with kindness.
Activity: Using puppets, the teacher will act out a puppet feeling sad at the block corner. Children will suggest kind responses — asking 'Are you okay?', offering a toy, or getting a teacher — and practice saying one.
Materials: Puppets; response picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A sentence frame ('Are you okay?') and response cards to choose from.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Graph how our class feels today.
Activity: At morning check-in, each child will place their name card under the feeling that matches their morning. We will count each column together and say which feeling has the most friends today.
Materials: Feelings check-in chart; name cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A quiet check-in with the teacher instead of in front of the group, if a child prefers.

Creative Art — Goal: Draw faces that show different feelings.
Activity: Children will choose a feeling and draw it on a paper-plate face — eyebrows up for surprised, mouth down for sad. The teacher will label each plate with the feeling word the child names.
Materials: Paper plates; crayons
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Face-feature stickers to position instead of drawing, for children frustrated by drawing.

Music / Movement — Goal: Sing a feelings song with actions for each verse.
Activity: We will sing 'If You're Happy and You Know It' and add new verses — if you're sad and you know it, hug yourself; if you're mad and you know it, take a breath. Children will follow the action for each feeling.
Materials: Teacher-led song; feelings cards as cues
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Feeling cards held up before each verse so children can get ready for the action.

Motor Activities — Goal: Build feeling faces on playdough mats.
Activity: Children will press and roll playdough to add eyes, eyebrows, and mouths to laminated face mats, changing the face from happy to surprised to sleepy.
Materials: Laminated face mats; playdough; small rollers
Grouping: Centers — fine motor table
Support: Pre-rolled dough pieces and dough tools for children who need help forming features.

Technology — Goal: Capture a feeling face with the class camera.
Activity: With the teacher, children who wish will choose a feeling and make the face while the teacher takes their photo. We will view the photos together and guess each feeling.
Materials: Class tablet (teacher-held); projector
Grouping: Small groups; teacher-led
Support: Children may photograph a puppet making the face instead of being photographed themselves.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Play feelings freeze dance outside.
Activity: Outside, children will move to music and, when it stops, freeze and show the feeling on the card the teacher holds up — using their whole bodies, not just their faces.
Materials: Portable speaker; feelings cards; open playground space
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A defined space spot and a buddy to freeze beside, for children who need a clear boundary.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn that all feelings are okay and feelings change.
Activity: We will talk about feelings being like weather — they come, they stay a while, and they pass. Each child may share a feeling they had today that already changed.
Materials: Feelings chart; weather picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A feelings card to hold up instead of speaking, for children who find sharing hard.

title: All About Me: When Feelings Are Big
subject: SEL
description: Preschool day plan from the 'All About Me' thematic week (September): When Feelings Are Big. Focus book: The Color Monster — Anna Llenas. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: The Color Monster — Anna Llenas

Language Arts — Goal: Sort feelings by the colors in the story and retell how they got mixed up.
Activity: We will read the focus book, then help sort pom-pom 'feelings' into labeled jars — yellow for happiness, blue for sadness, red for anger, green for calm. Children will retell how the monster's feelings became untangled.
Materials: Focus book; clear jars with feelings labels; colored pom-poms
Grouping: Large group then small groups — carpet/science table
Support: Just two jars at a time for children who are new to sorting by an idea instead of a look.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Explore colors mixing and spreading like feelings do.
Activity: Children will draw with washable markers on coffee filters, then use droppers of water to watch the colors spread and blend. We will connect the swirling colors to how feelings can mix together.
Materials: Coffee filters; washable markers; droppers; water cups; trays
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: A larger-bulb dropper for easier squeezing, and extra time to watch the colors move.

Social Science — Goal: Practice using our calm-down corner tools.
Activity: We will visit the calm-down corner together and try each tool: a breathing card, a squeeze ball, a quiet picture book, and a soft cushion. Each child will choose the tool they would like to use when feelings feel big.
Materials: Calm-down corner tools; choice board
Grouping: Small groups — calm corner; teacher-guided
Support: Adult proximity during the visit, and a visual choice board the child can use all year.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Sort and count feelings pom-poms by color.
Activity: Children will sort the mixed pom-poms into color jars, count how many are in each jar, and use number cards to label the amounts. We will say which jar has the most.
Materials: Pom-poms; jars; number cards
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: Counting together with a partner and a number line strip to check the order.

Creative Art — Goal: Draw my feelings in colors and lines.
Activity: On big paper, children will choose colors for how they feel today and fill the page with scribbles, swirls, or shapes. The teacher will write each child's own words about their picture on the back.
Materials: Large paper; crayons and oil pastels
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A choice of chunky pastels and crayons, and the message that there is no right way for the picture to look.

Music / Movement — Goal: Move my body to show calm and excited.
Activity: We will move with scarves to slow music — floating and swaying for calm — then march to fast music for excited. When the music stops, everyone will take one slow breath before the next round.
Materials: Scarves; recorded music (slow and fast)
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A seated scarf option and a defined movement spot for children who need one.

Motor Activities — Goal: Use heavy work to help my body reset.
Activity: Children will carry beanbag 'feelings jars' across the room to a shelf, then do wall push-ups with the teacher counting. We will talk about how pushing and carrying helps big feelings settle.
Materials: Beanbags; shelf; mats
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: Lighter beanbags and a shorter carrying distance, so every child can finish successfully.

Technology — Goal: Record a feelings message in my own voice.
Activity: Children will record the sentence 'I feel ___ when ___.' into the class recorder, with the teacher's help. We will listen to our messages at closing circle and cheer for each speaker.
Materials: Voice recorder or tablet with recording app
Grouping: Small group — quiet corner; teacher-guided
Support: Recording together with a partner or echoing the teacher's voice for confidence.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Take a breathing walk on the garden path.
Activity: Outside, we will walk the garden path slowly and stop at three 'breathing spots' to smell the air and breathe out long and slow. Children will share one thing they noticed at each stop.
Materials: Garden path; breathing-spot signs
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A buddy to walk with and the option of a shorter loop back to the classroom.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn that asking for help with feelings is brave.
Activity: A puppet's feelings will get all mixed up in a short teacher skit, and the puppet will practice saying, 'I need help, please.' Children will practice the words and learn they can hand any teacher a help card, too.
Materials: Puppets; help cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A help card to hand to an adult instead of speaking, available to every child from now on.

title: All About Me: My Family

description: Preschool day plan from the 'All About Me' thematic week (September): My Family. Focus book: The Family Book — Todd Parr. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: The Family Book — Todd Parr

Language Arts — Goal: Describe who is in my family.
Activity: After reading the focus book, children will draw the people (and pets) in their family and dictate labels for each person. The pages will become part of our class family book.
Materials: Focus book; drawing paper; crayons
Grouping: Large group then independent — carpet/tables
Support: People-shaped stamps and stickers for children who find drawing figures frustrating.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Match baby animals to their parents.
Activity: Children will look at animal family photos and match each baby animal to its parent — chick to hen, calf to cow, kitten to cat — and say what clues helped them decide.
Materials: Animal family photo cards
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Fewer matches per round (start with three pairs) for children building matching stamina.

Social Science — Goal: Share my family page and learn how families differ.
Activity: In small groups, children will show their family pages and tell one thing their family likes to do together. The teacher will chart our ideas under 'Families like to...'.
Materials: Family pages from Language Arts; chart paper
Grouping: Small groups — tables; teacher-guided
Support: Sharing just with the teacher if a child prefers not to share with the group.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count the people in my family and graph our family sizes.
Activity: Children will count the people in their family drawing, then place a marker on our class graph at that number. We will count the markers in each column and talk about the different sizes of families.
Materials: Family drawings; class graph chart; markers
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Counters matched one-to-one onto the drawing to help with the counting.

Creative Art — Goal: Make a paper house with my family inside.
Activity: Children will color and decorate a paper house, then draw their family members in the windows and doorway. Finished houses will line our hallway bulletin board.
Materials: Paper house templates (pre-folded available); crayons; glue
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A pre-folded, pre-assembled house for children who need to skip the folding steps.

Music / Movement — Goal: Sing the finger family song.
Activity: We will sing the finger family song, holding up one finger for each family member as they are 'called.' Children may name their own family members in the final verse with the teacher's help.
Materials: Teacher-led song; finger puppet set
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Finger puppets to wear for children who have trouble isolating fingers.

Motor Activities — Goal: Cut along lines to separate family pictures.
Activity: Children will cut along wide straight lines to separate a strip of family pictures, then arrange their cards from biggest person to smallest. The teacher will be close by for scissor support.
Materials: Safety scissors; family picture strips
Grouping: Centers — fine motor table; teacher-supervised
Support: Loop scissors, thicker paper, or a tearing alternative for children still learning to cut.

Technology — Goal: Listen to a story about a family at the listening center.
Activity: At the listening center, children will follow along with a recorded story about a family, turning the pages at the chime and looking at the pictures as the narrator reads.
Materials: Listening center; recorded story with book copies; headphones
Grouping: Centers — pairs; child-led after setup
Support: Headphones adjusted by the teacher and a bookmark showing where to start.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Play a family helpers relay outdoors.
Activity: Teams will carry soft 'groceries' (beanbags) one at a time across the playground to a 'home' mat, working together until every bag is home. We will cheer for helpers, not winners.
Materials: Beanbags; baskets; home mats
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-supervised
Support: A shorter carrying distance and a partner carry for children who need support.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Feel grateful for the people who care for me.
Activity: Each child will name or draw one thing someone in their family does that helps them — cooking, hugging, reading stories — and add a heart to our gratitude board.
Materials: Heart cutouts; gratitude board; crayons
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Drawing instead of telling, and picture choices to spark an idea.
