Support: A choice of three picture thank-you cards to name, for children unsure what to say.

Grouping: Pairs — carpet
Support: Children choose their recipient from picture cards (friend, teacher, family) to make the choice concrete.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count letters in names and compare lengths.
Activity: Children will count the letters in their first name with letter tiles, compare who has more or fewer, and line up name cards from fewest letters to most.
Materials: Letter tiles; name cards; comparison mat
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: Name cards to copy from for children not yet writing letters independently.

Creative Art — Goal: Create a picture-letter with a drawing, a name, and a stamp.
Activity: Children will draw a picture-letter for a classmate: a drawing, their name mark, and one sticker stamp in the corner, designing the whole page the way real mail art looks.
Materials: Paper; crayons; sticker stamps
Grouping: Art center / writing center, groups of 4–5
Support: Thick crayons and a name tracer sheet for children building letter formation.

Music / Movement — Goal: Recognize letters while moving to a song.
Activity: We will sing an ABC song while pointing to giant letter cards scattered on the rug; when the music pauses, children find and stand beside the letter the teacher calls.
Materials: Giant letter cards; recorded ABC song
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Picture cue cards for each letter as it comes up in the song.

Motor Activities — Goal: Cut along lines and seal envelopes with glue sticks.
Activity: At the writing table children will practice cutting along straight and zigzag lines to separate 'stamps' from their sticker sheets, and squeezing glue sticks to seal flip-open paper envelopes.
Materials: Safety scissors; stamp sheets to cut; paper envelopes; glue sticks
Grouping: Centers — writing table
Support: Spring-loaded scissors and a teacher nearby for children learning to open and close blades.

Technology — Goal: Photograph our work to share with families.
Activity: Children will photograph their finished letters with the class tablet (teacher-assisted) to make a 'Letters We Wrote' slideshow for families at pickup.
Materials: Class tablet; finished letters
Grouping: Small groups; teacher-guided
Support: Teacher handles the camera; the child frames the shot by pointing and saying 'now.'

Outdoor Education — Goal: Form giant letters outdoors with chalk and body movement.
Activity: Outside, children will 'write' giant letters in chalk on the pavement — the first letter of their name as big as they can — and walk its shape with their feet.

Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A defined chalk frame to draw inside for children who want a boundary.

Activity: The Postman carries apologies, thank-yous, and party invitations — feelings in envelopes. We will talk about how writing can say things that are hard to say out loud, like 'I'm sorry' or 'I miss you.'
Materials: Focus book (favorite letter page); feelings cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A sentence frame ('I feel ___ when...') with emotion pictures for emerging speakers.

title: Post Office & Letter Writing: Stamps, Envelopes, and Addresses
subject: ELA / Reading
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Post Office & Letter Writing' thematic week (February): Stamps, Envelopes, and Addresses. Focus book: Dear Juno — Soyung Pak. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Dear Juno — Soyung Pak

Language Arts — Goal: Read a simple address and understand letters can carry pictures too.
Activity: We will read about Juno, who 'reads' a letter from his grandmother across the ocean by its drawings, then decode our classroom address together line by line — name, street, town — on the big envelope.
Materials: Focus book; big teaching envelope; address poster
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: An enlarged address poster with each line color-coded for children learning the parts.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Mix and test a simple paste: what makes it sticky?
Activity: Children will mix flour-and-water paste with the teacher's recipe help, brush it on paper strips, and test which strip sticks best to an envelope — homemade glue science (teacher supervises; no tasting).
Materials: Flour; water; bowls; brushes; paper strips
Grouping: Small groups — science table; teacher-guided
Support: Smaller cups of mixture and an adult holding the tray steady for children pouring.

Social Science — Goal: Locate faraway and nearby places on a globe.
Activity: Using Dear Juno's faraway grandmother as our start, we will find Korea and our own town on the globe, and talk about how mail connects families who live far apart in many different places.
Materials: Globe; focus book; map pins (teacher-placed)
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Picture sorting cards instead of country names for children joining by matching images.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count play money to match a number up to 10.
Activity: Children will count out play coins to 'buy' a stamp priced at a number of cents shown on a card (up to 10), matching coins to the price exactly.
Materials: Play coins; price cards 1–10; stamp stickers
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: A 1–10 number strip to count along for children building correspondence.

Creative Art — Goal: Design a postage stamp with perforated edges.
Activity: Children will design their own postage stamps inside perforated-edge frames — drawing something they love — then edge them with hole-punch dots to look like real stamps.
Materials: Stamp frames; crayons; hole punches; glue
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Larger stamp outlines for children who need more room for details.

Music / Movement — Goal: Tell a journey with whole-body movements in sequence.
Activity: We will act out a 'letter's long journey' movement story: stamp (stomp), fly (arms wide over the ocean like Juno's grandmother's letter), sail, and finally slide into a mailbox.
Materials: Movement story prompts; open space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Slower spins and holding the teacher's hand option for children who get dizzy easily.

Motor Activities — Goal: Press, stack, and carry — building hand and arm strength.
Activity: At the postmark station, children will press stamp pads and postmark stamps onto envelopes with two hands, stack them in piles of five, and deliver piles to the sorting table.
Materials: Ink pads (washable); postmark stamps; envelopes
Grouping: Centers — writing table
Support: A seated stamping option at the table edge for children who prefer not to stand in line.

Technology — Goal: Compose a class email with the teacher — mail that travels fast.
Activity: With the teacher typing, each child will add one line to a class email to a partner preschool class (arranged by the teacher), and we will press 'send' together and talk about how email is mail that travels by computer.
Materials: Tablet or classroom computer; teacher account
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Teacher types; the child chooses the words by pointing to picture options.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Find and identify numbers in the outdoor environment.
Activity: Outside, we will hunt for numbers around the school — on doors, signs, and the building address — and chalk the numbers we find on the pavement number line.
Materials: Clipboards; chalk
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A magnifier and gloves provided for children who like tools for looking closely.

Activity: Stamps carry tiny pictures of places and things people are proud of. Children will share what they drew on their stamp and one kind word about a friend's stamp, practicing giving compliments.
Materials: Children's stamp art; compliment sentence frame
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: The option to dictate a caption for their displayed stamp for children whose drawing outruns their words.

title: Post Office & Letter Writing: The Mail Carrier's Route
subject: ELA / Reading
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Post Office & Letter Writing' thematic week (February): The Mail Carrier's Route. Focus book: A Day with the Mail Carrier — — a photo nonfiction picture book following a mail carrier through one busy day (substitute any community-helper title on hand). Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: A Day with the Mail Carrier — — a photo nonfiction picture book following a mail carrier through one busy day (substitute any community-helper title on hand)

Language Arts — Goal: Sequence a worker's day and use job vocabulary.
Activity: We will read a carrier's day from first pickup to last doorstep, sequence route pictures (post office, truck, street, mailbox), and learn route words: deliver, collect, sort.
Materials: Focus book; route picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Picture route cards to hold and follow for children who need the story in their hands.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Test how carriers protect mail from weather.
Activity: Carriers deliver in all weather, so we will test our paper letters: one left plain, one in a plastic sleeve, one in a zip bag, sprinkled with 'rain' — and check which letter stayed dry inside.
Materials: Paper letters; plastic sleeves; zip bags; spray bottle
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Weather picture cards at each station so the plan is visible before touching materials.

Social Science — Goal: Identify the different jobs on a postal team.
Activity: We will set up the jobs of a postal team — sorter, driver, carrier, clerk — and children will pick a job badge, try the job at its station, then rotate so everyone tries two jobs.
Materials: Job badges; sorting bins; toy truck; counter bell
Grouping: Centers — dramatic play and tables; teacher-guided
Support: A job badge and role card so children can enter play by choosing a pictured role.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Deliver mail in number order 1–10 (ordinal practice).
Activity: Children will deliver number-card letters to matching numbered 'houses' in order along a floor street, counting houses aloud as the truck 'drives.'
Materials: Numbered house cards; floor street tape; letter cards
Grouping: Small groups — movement/math area
Support: A number path mat so children can move a counter along the numbers as they count.

Creative Art — Goal: Construct a mail truck from a recycled box.
Activity: Children will build mail trucks from cereal boxes — painting them, adding paper wheels and a roof slot — and drive them on the block-area road when dry.
Materials: Cereal boxes; paint; paper circles; glue; smocks
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A pre-cut simple truck outline available for children who want to decorate rather than construct.

Music / Movement — Goal: Keep a steady walking beat and respond to a chime cue.
Activity: We will learn a 'walking route' rhythm song: steady walking beats in the verses, doorbell 'ding-dong' chimes (xylophone) in the chorus, freezing at each 'door.'
Materials: Xylophone; recorded walking-tempo song
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: The xylophone played from a seated spot beside the teacher for children who prefer it.

Motor Activities — Goal: Carry a load while stepping over and up obstacles.
Activity: Wearing carrier bags, children will follow an indoor obstacle route: step over curb lines, climb two steps to a 'porch,' post the letter, and walk the loop again carrying an empty bag.
Materials: Carrier bags; step stools; tape curbs; letters
Grouping: Small groups — gym area; teacher-supervised
Support: A lighter bag and a short route option for children building carrying endurance.

Technology — Goal: See how machines help sort mail (teacher-selected video).
Activity: Children will watch short teacher-selected clips of real sorting machines moving letters quickly along belts, then compare with our slow hand-sorting and say what the machine does faster.
Materials: Projector/screen; teacher-selected clip
Grouping: Small group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Pre-set clips bookmarked by the teacher so a child only presses play.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Follow a real outdoor route with stops in order.
Activity: We will follow a short walking route on school grounds like a carrier: from the office door along the path to three 'stops' (flagpole, garden gate, front sign), delivering a pretend letter at each.
Materials: Pretend letters; route stops marked with signs
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: An adult walking point with children who need support navigating the route.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Practice patience and gratitude for people who serve our neighborhood.
Activity: Carriers walk their routes in sun, rain, and cold, and neighbors say thank you. We will practice waiting for our turn on the route game and saying a real thank-you to our own school mail staff when we see them.
Materials: Feelings chart; thank-you card supplies
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Specific praise naming the patience we saw, for children learning to wait.

subject: ELA / Reading

evidence:
Focus book: A Letter to Amy — Ezra Jack Keats

Language Arts — Goal: Write a real invitation letter for a class event.
Activity: We will read how Peter writes a birthday invitation, then each child will make an invitation letter to our Friday classroom celebration, addressing it to their own cubby mailbox for delivery day.
Materials: Focus book; invitation cards; envelopes; class mailbox list
Grouping: Writing center, small groups; teacher support
Support: Word cards and a sentence frame ('Please come to...') for children composing their first invitations.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Explore magnetism with post office materials.
Activity: Children will test which mailbox items are magnetic (paper clips, metal stamps) with magnet wands, charting results — the science hiding inside our post office tools.
Materials: Magnet wands; paper clips; stamps; sorting chart
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: A lighter magnet wand for children with less hand strength, and a raised tray edge to keep pieces in reach.

Social Science — Goal: Run a classroom post office: taking turns in real roles.
Activity: Our post office opens for business: children take shifts as clerk, sorter, and carrier while 'customers' from our class (and a visiting teacher) buy stamps, post letters, and ask for help finding a mailbox.
Materials: Post office setup; play money; stamp stickers; uniforms (bags, caps)
Grouping: Centers — dramatic play; extended play period
Support: An adult greeter at the door to introduce shy children to their first 'customer.'

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Tally and graph our classroom mail deliveries.
Activity: We will open our post office with a counting day: children stamp and count every letter delivered today on our tally board, graphing deliveries by day of the week at closing time.
Materials: Tally board; delivered letters; graph chart
Grouping: Whole class — post office center
Support: Counting with a partner and a hundreds-chart corner visible for children reaching beyond 10.

Creative Art — Goal: Make a post office mural with printed postmarks.
Activity: Children will print postmark art with circle stamps and date stamps on big paper, overlapping marks the way real cancelled mail looks, to decorate our post office wall.
Materials: Circle stamps; date stamps; ink pads; big paper
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Stamps with handles and pre-mixed colors for children who want quick success.

Music / Movement — Goal: Celebrate with a stop-and-deliver movement game.
Activity: Our opening celebration includes the 'Special Delivery' dance: children dance with a letter held high, deliver it to a mailbox when the music stops, and freeze for a cheer.
Materials: Recorded music; letters; mailboxes
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: The option to deliver letters from a seated 'clerk' chair during the dance for children joining in their own way.

Motor Activities — Goal: Complete a multi-step delivery job in order.
Activity: At the opening, children will run the delivery relay: sort letters into street bins, load the wagon truck, walk the route, and post each letter in the right class mailbox.
Materials: Sorting bins; wagon; class mailboxes; letters
Grouping: Small groups — whole room; teacher-supervised
Support: Seated sorting trays for children who work best sitting, with the same job and badge.

Technology — Goal: Document our post office opening with photos and captions.
Activity: Children will use the class camera (teacher-assisted) to document opening day — the first customer, the first delivery — and dictate captions for our class newsletter photo page.
Materials: Class camera or tablet; newsletter template
Grouping: Small groups; teacher-guided
Support: Teacher presses shutter for children who direct the photo by choosing the moment.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Deliver real thank-you letters along an outdoor route.
Activity: For a final route, we will deliver teacher-written thank-you letters to real stops around the school grounds — the office door basket, the garden sign, the library window box (arranged with staff) — walking the full route together.
Materials: Prepared thank-you letters; route baskets
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: Buddy delivery pairs for the outdoor run so no child goes alone.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Practice including everyone — no mailbox left empty.
Activity: Peter's invitation taught us that including everyone feels better than leaving someone out. We will make sure every classmate's mailbox receives at least one kind letter today — checking our list together like careful friends.
Materials: Class mailbox list; extra letter supplies
Grouping: Whole class — carpet and post office
Support: A quiet corner mailbox for children who would rather receive their letter privately.

title: Dinosaurs: Meet the Dinosaurs
subject: Science
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Dinosaurs' thematic week (March): Meet the Dinosaurs. Focus book: How Do Dinosaurs Say Good Night? — Jane Yolen. evidence:
Focus book: How Do Dinosaurs Say Good Night? — Jane Yolen

Language Arts — Goal: Answer questions about a story and share ideas in complete ideas.
Activity: We will read the focus book and answer its questions out loud together — does a dinosaur stomp his feet? Children will say what the dinosaurs in the book do and what they think our classroom dinosaurs did long ago.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led

Activity: Children will sort animal cards into 'alive today,' 'alive long ago (dinosaurs),' and 'make-believe' (dragons), and we will talk about how scientists know dinosaurs were real from bones left behind.

Grouping: Small groups — science table; teacher-guided
Support: Picture word cards ('long ago,' 'extinct,' 'fossil') to use while sorting.

Social Science — Goal: Work with a partner to sort by observable features.
Activity: Children will work in pairs to sort dinosaur pictures into 'gentle plant-eaters' and 'meat-eaters' using clues from teeth and feet, then share one clue they used.
Materials: Dinosaur picture cards; sorting mats; magnifiers
Grouping: Pairs — tables; teacher circulates
Support: Partner sorting so children can talk through the big and small choices together.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Sort dinosaurs by size and count sets up to 10.
Activity: Children will count toy dinosaurs into numbered 'nests,' then order the dinosaurs by size from smallest to biggest and check their line with a partner.
Materials: Toy dinosaurs; numbered nest mats; size-order cards
Grouping: Centers — math area; child-led after demo
Support: Large dinosaurs and a number line floor mat for children who need bigger anchors.

Creative Art — Goal: Paint a large shape with sponges, filling the space.
Activity: Children will sponge-paint a big dinosaur silhouette, choosing greens, browns, and oranges and talking about what colors they think dinosaurs might have been.
Materials: Dinosaur silhouette paper; sponge brushes; paint; smocks
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Chunky brushes and a damp-sponge option for children who prefer less mess.

Music / Movement — Goal: Move heavily and lightly in response to a beat (loud/soft, fast/slow).
Activity: We will stomp, tiptoe, and freeze like dinosaurs to a drumbeat: heavy stomps for the big dinosaurs, quiet tip-toes for the small ones, and a freeze when the drum stops.
Materials: Hand drum; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A 'safe island' mat to rest on if the stomping game gets too exciting.

Motor Activities — Goal: Follow a footprint path with balance and control.
Activity: Children will step from footprint to footprint laid across the floor, matching their feet to the big dinosaur prints and walking heel-to-toe on the narrow ones.
Materials: Large paper or foam footprints; open floor space
Grouping: Large group in turns — movement area
Support: A shorter path between footprints for children with smaller strides or mobility supports.

Technology — Goal: Use a digital microscope to look closely at natural objects.
Activity: With the teacher, children will look at a piece of real bark, a feather, and an eggshell under the digital microscope and compare them to dinosaur skin, feathers, and eggs in our picture books.
Materials: Digital microscope; bark; feather; eggshell; picture books
Grouping: Small groups — science table; teacher-led
Support: Teacher holds the microscope steady while the child describes what they see.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Compare sizes in nature (bigger than, smaller than).
Activity: On our walk, children will look for the biggest and smallest things they can find outside — a tall tree, a tiny pebble — and we will compare them to our book's dinosaurs: bigger than a car? smaller than a shoe?
Materials: Clipboards; crayons; playground and garden route
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A shorter search loop staying near the building for children who tire.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Name feelings big and small, and one way to calm down.
Activity: Even though the book's dinosaurs make big messes, their families still love them — we will talk about how everyone has big feelings sometimes, and name one thing we can do to feel calm at bedtime and at school.
Materials: Focus book; feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A fidget kept in laps for children who need movement to listen.

title: Dinosaurs: Big and Small, Long Ago

Grouping: Small group — math center

Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Body-percussion-only roles (claps and pats) for children still coordinating sticks.

Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised

Support: Headphones shared with a partner who helps with the controls.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led

title: Dinosaurs: Fossil Hunters
subject: Science
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Dinosaurs' thematic week (March): Fossil Hunters. Focus book: Fossils Tell a Story — — a simple nonfiction picture book about how fossils are found and what bones tell us (substitute any fossil title on hand). Language Arts — Goal: Learn and use science vocabulary: fossil, dig, bone, extinct.
Activity: We will read the focus book and add four scientist words to our word wall, practicing saying and using them while we describe our own dig at the sensory bin.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led

Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Break a demonstration piece first so every child sees the layers before starting.

Grouping: Centers — dramatic play/science area

Activity: Diggers will count the 'bones' they uncover in the dig bin, record the count with tally marks, and compare piles to find who uncovered more and fewer.

Grouping: Centers — sensory/science area; child-led after demo
Support: Number stamps available so counting, not numeral writing, is the focus.

Creative Art — Goal: Make prints in clay to create a fossil.
Activity: Children will press shells, toy bones, and textured objects into clay or salt dough to make fossil prints, lift them carefully, and let the 'fossils' dry for our museum.
Materials: Clay or salt dough; shells; toy bones; textured objects; trays
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A thicker dough ball and a rolling pin with handles for children building hand strength.

Music / Movement — Goal: Move through a sequence of actions and freeze on cue.
Activity: We will move like paleontologists on a dig to music: walk the site, kneel and brush, lift a heavy bone with a partner, and freeze in a 'statue fossil' pose when the music stops.
Materials: Recorded music; action picture cards
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Rest spots marked off the 'dig' area for children who need a break from group movement.

Motor Activities — Goal: Strengthen pencil grasp with tracing and rubbings.
Activity: Children will trace dinosaur outlines, bones, and footprint rubbings with crayons, pressing hard and light to make the textures appear.
Materials: Texture plates; dinosaur outlines; crayons; paper
Grouping: Centers — fine motor table
Support: A slant board and a short crayon for children developing pencil grasp.

Technology — Goal: Sequence photos of a process and narrate the steps.
Activity: Children will sort photos of our fossil prints — dough, pressing, lifting, finished fossil — into order on the tablet slideshow, telling the steps as they swipe.
Materials: Tablet with teacher-taken photos; projector (optional)
Grouping: Small groups; teacher-guided
Support: A simple two-photo sequence for children who need fewer images to order.

Activity: Outside in our digging patch (or large sand area), children will dig gently with trowels and brushes, sifting for shells, smooth stones, and leaf shapes, and lay finds in a row to examine.

Grouping: Whole class — outdoors, in small groups
Support: A seated dig spot with a raised bin for children who can't kneel comfortably.

Activity: Paleontologists sometimes dig all day and find nothing — we will talk about not giving up when something is hard, and practice one more careful try on a tricky puzzle before asking for help.

Grouping: Large group then small groups — carpet/tables
Support: A two-minute sand timer for children learning to wait for a find.

Activity: We will read the focus book and build a labeled dinosaur diagram together on chart paper — teeth, tail, spikes, claws — then children will label one body part on their own dinosaur picture.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Choice of dinosaur picture cards to label for children building vocabulary.

Activity: Children will compare dinosaur features to animals alive today: thick elephant skin, ostrich legs, turtle shell, lizard tail — matching cards and finding real photos that show the same feature.

Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Real objects paired with each card so the comparison is concrete, not abstract.

Activity: Children will choose a dinosaur to move like — heavy stomper, long-neck reacher, fast runner, swimmer — and the class will guess from the movements and sounds, no words allowed.

Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Sentence frames ('I move like...') and a partner to move with.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Compare weights and sort sets, counting each group.
Activity: Children will compare dinosaur figures on a balance scale — which is heavier? — then group dinosaurs into 'two legs' and 'four legs' sets and count each group.
Materials: Balance scale; toy dinosaurs; sorting mats
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: A balance with block 'weights' added one at a time alongside the child.

Creative Art — Goal: Print dinosaur spikes and footprints with sponge shapes.
Activity: Children will cut (or use pre-cut) sponge shapes to print a dinosaur scene — spikes down a back, footprints across the ground — choosing where each print goes.
Materials: Sponges; paint trays; large paper; scissors (teacher pre-cuts some)
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Halved sponges that fit small palms for better control of the print.

Music / Movement — Goal: Listen for a signal word before moving (inhibitory control).
Activity: We will play 'Dino Says': movements come only when Dino says so — Dino says stomp, Dino says stretch tall like a long neck, Dino says curl up small in an egg.
Materials: Teacher voice cues; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Chime-only option for children sensitive to louder drum sounds.

Motor Activities — Goal: Carry an object with two hands while walking a course.
Activity: Children will stomp-walk a chalk path carrying a big paper 'egg' on a spoon with two hands, keeping it steady around the cones and back to the nest.
Materials: Paper eggs; large spoons; cones; nest basket
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A long-handled grabber for children who need reach support.

Technology — Goal: Document a collection with photos and count the results.
Activity: Two children at a time will take our 'museum camera' (tablet) on a dinosaur walk around the room, photographing every dinosaur they can find in our displays, then count the photos with the class.
Materials: Tablet camera; classroom dino displays
Grouping: Pairs, rotating; teacher-guided
Support: A partner to take the walk with and turns counted on a timer.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Compare our bodies' movement to a giant dinosaur's stride.
Activity: Children will compare their own stride to a taped-out dinosaur stride on the playground (chalk marks 6 feet apart), jumping and stretching to try to match one giant step.
Materials: Chalk; measuring tape (teacher); playground
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A stuffed dinosaur buddy to carry for children who need comfort outdoors.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Practice a calming breath to use with big feelings.
Activity: We will notice how dinosaurs in stories roar when they feel big things, and practice our own 'dino breaths' — a big inhale, then a slow roar-out — to use when we feel frustrated or excited.
Materials: Feelings chart; focus book (roaring page)
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A feelings-faces pointer for children who express emotions better by showing than saying.

Grouping: Whole class in small groups — around the room

Focus book: Humpty Dumpty and Other Rhymes — — a classic illustrated collection of traditional nursery rhymes (substitute any Mother Goose collection on hand)

Language Arts — Goal: Chant a rhyme and clap its rhythm, noticing rhyming words.
Activity: We will read and chant 'Humpty Dumpty' together with big voices and small voices, clapping on 'wall' and 'fall.' Children will listen for the word pairs that sound the same at the ends of lines.
Materials: Focus book; rhyming word cards (wall/fall, king/ring)
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Picture cards for the rhyme's key words so children can follow the story even if the old-fashioned words are new.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Predict and observe what happens when eggs drop (teacher keeps real eggs high and safe).
Activity: Children will predict whether a plastic egg, a wooden egg, and a real egg (teacher-handled only, dropped into a deep tub of sand) will crack, then observe and sort the results on our chart — just like wondering about Humpty.
Materials: Plastic and wooden eggs; one real egg (teacher only); deep sand tub; chart
Grouping: Small groups — science table; teacher-led demo
Support: Children drop the plastic and wooden eggs from a low step stool for a hands-on turn at a safe height.

Social Science — Goal: Talk about helping someone who has had a fall or a hard moment.
Activity: In the rhyme, all the king's horses and men couldn't help Humpty — we will brainstorm what helpers today CAN do: get a grown-up, bring a bandage, sit with a friend, and practice offering help kindly.
Materials: Helper picture cards; feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Partner brainstorm before whole-group sharing so quieter voices get heard first.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Build and read AB and ABB patterns.
Activity: Children will build Humpty's wall with red and white paper 'bricks' in a pattern strip (red-white-red-white), then try a harder wall (red-red-white) and read their pattern to a friend.
Materials: Paper brick strips; crayons; pattern cards
Grouping: Centers — math area; child-led after demo
Support: A finished pattern strip to copy for children new to patterning; loose bricks for free building after.

Creative Art — Goal: Assemble a character from shapes and add details.
Activity: Children will glue an oval Humpty body onto a brick-patterned wall, then draw his legs, arms, face, and clothes, telling the teacher one detail they added.
Materials: Oval cut-outs; brick-pattern paper; glue; markers
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Pre-glued wall backgrounds for children who want to start with the character right away.

Music / Movement — Goal: Act out a rhyme's actions in order and freeze at the fall.
Activity: We will chant the rhyme while acting: sit tall on the 'wall' (a bench), sway, and on 'fall' slide safely to a cushion and freeze, then 'horses and men' gallop in to check on us.
Materials: Low bench; cushions; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A sitting-on-the-floor 'wall' option for children who should not climb on the bench.

Motor Activities — Goal: Balance objects while walking a short path.
Activity: Children will carry a plastic egg on a large spoon along a tape path to the 'wall' and back, using two hands and slow feet.
Materials: Plastic eggs; large spoons; tape path
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: The egg rests in a small cup on the spoon for children who need a sturdier start.

Technology — Goal: Listen to rhymes at the listening center and track print with a pointer.
Activity: Children will listen to a recording of Mother Goose rhymes while following in the big book with a pointer, turning the page at the chime.
Materials: Listening center; recorded rhymes; big book; pointer
Grouping: Centers — pairs; child-led after setup
Support: A bookmark that shows which page we are on for children who lose their place.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Build a 'wall' outdoors and test what rolls off it safely.
Activity: Outside, children will stack large soft blocks into a low wall, sit a stuffed Humpty on top, and experiment with soft balls rolling down a ramp beside it — noticing which land softly.
Materials: Soft outdoor blocks; stuffed egg toy; balls; ramp board
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors, in small groups
Support: Blocks placed at ground level for children building from a seated position.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn that everyone falls sometimes, and getting help is brave.
Activity: We will talk about times we fell or something broke, how it felt, and what helped; each child will finish the sentence 'When I fall, I can...' and we will add the ideas to a class poster.
Materials: Class poster; markers; feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Picture choices (get a grown-up, take a breath, ask for a hug) for children who need ideas to choose from.

title: Nursery Rhymes: Itsy Bitsy Spider
subject: ELA / Reading
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Nursery Rhymes' thematic week (March): Itsy Bitsy Spider. Focus book: The Itsy Bitsy Spider — Iza Trapani. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: The Itsy Bitsy Spider — Iza Trapani

Language Arts — Goal: Retell a rhyme's journey in order with hand motions.
Activity: We will sing and read the extended version of the rhyme, following the spider through the whole house adventure and back outside, using hand motions for climb, rain, and sun, then retell the journey to a partner in order.
Materials: Focus book; journey picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Journey cards kept in view as a story map for children retelling the sequence.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Observe how water moves and what it washes away.
Activity: At the water table, children will pour water down tilted gutter 'spouts' and watch light paper spiders wash down, then see them 'climb' again when the water stops — rain and sun in our own spout.
Materials: Water table; gutter sections; paper spiders; pitchers
Grouping: Centers — science area; child-led after demo
Support: A small pitcher with a handle for control; dry paper spiders as spares when one tears.

Social Science — Goal: Identify weather words and what we do for each kind of weather.
Activity: Children will sort weather picture cards under 'rain' and 'sun,' telling what the spider (and we) do in each: shelter and wait, or come out and climb.
Materials: Weather picture cards; sorting mats
Grouping: Small groups — tables
Support: Partner sorting with the teacher's model pair already in place to study.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count up and back down to 8 (spider legs) in a number path.
Activity: Children will walk a numbered floor path shaped like a spout, counting steps up to 8, being 'washed' back to the bottom, and counting back down — spider-leg counting both ways.
Materials: Numbered floor path 1–8; spider pointer
Grouping: Large group in turns — movement area
Support: Counting with a partner who points to each number as it's said.

Creative Art — Goal: Create a spider with eight legs using lines and symmetry ideas.
Activity: Children will paint a round spider body, then add eight legs with black paint and thin brushes — four on each side — counting as they go and checking both sides match.
Materials: Paint; circle papers; thin brushes; wiggly eyes
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Eight pre-drawn leg dots to connect for children who lose count while painting.

Music / Movement — Goal: Sing the rhyme with coordinated finger motions.
Activity: We will sing 'Itsy Bitsy Spider' slowly, then fast, then whisper-quiet, practicing the thumb-to-finger climbing motion and the rain and sun actions in time with the words.
Materials: Teacher-led song; motion picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Big-arm climbing motions as an alternative for children still developing fine finger control.

Motor Activities — Goal: Climb up and come down classroom climbing equipment safely.
Activity: Children will climb up the low climber steps and slide or step down, 'just like the spider,' taking turns and waiting for a clear space below.
Materials: Low indoor climber or step blocks; mats
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: An adult hand offered for the way down for children who are still unsure.

Technology — Goal: Use a tablet with a teacher to watch a real spider in its web (short clip).
Activity: We will watch a brief, gentle nature clip of a spider building a web, pausing to count legs and notice how it climbs, then compare it to our rhyme spider.
Materials: Tablet or projector; teacher-selected clip
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Front seating and a heads-up that the spider is real but far away and friendly to watch.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Search for spider webs and spiders outdoors without disturbing them.
Activity: On a gentle hunt, children will look for webs in bushes and corners of the fence, point and count what they find, and draw one web in a nature journal — look with eyes, not hands.
Materials: Magnifiers; nature journals; crayons
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors, in small groups
Support: A photo of a web to compare finds against for children unsure what to look for.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn about trying again after something washes us back (persistence).
Activity: The spider doesn't stop when the rain comes — it climbs again. We will name one thing that is hard for us to do, and one small step we can take to climb again tomorrow.
Materials: Focus book; feelings chart; class poster
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Specific praise for each child who names their own 'climb again' step.

Observe how water moves and what it washes away

Sing the rhyme with coordinated finger motions

Search for spider webs and spiders outdoors without disturbing them
Learn about trying again after something washes us back (persistence)

title: Nursery Rhymes: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star
subject: ELA / Reading
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Nursery Rhymes' thematic week (March): Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star. Focus book: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star — Jane Taylor (classic rhyme); illustrated board-book editions widely available — substitute any starry-night title on hand. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star — Jane Taylor (classic rhyme); illustrated board-book editions widely available — substitute any starry-night title on hand

Language Arts — Goal: Notice that 'star' and 'are' rhyme; supply rhyming words in a chant.
Activity: We will sing the classic rhyme, holding up star cards on the word 'star,' and play a fill-in game: 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star, how I wonder what you...' as children shout the rhyming word.
Materials: Focus book; star word cards; chart of the rhyme
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Star cards to hold up as a response for children who don't yet join in singing.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Explore light and dark and how we see sparkle.
Activity: In a darkened corner tent, children will shine flashlights on foil stars, sequins, and matte paper, observing which materials twinkle back and which stay dull.
Materials: Flashlights; foil shapes; sequins; dark tent/blanket corner
Grouping: Small groups — science corner; teacher-supervised
Support: A lamp of one's own to control for children who need to be in charge of the light.

Social Science — Goal: Talk about nighttime routines and the people who work at night.
Activity: Children will sequence a bedtime picture set (dinner, bath, pajamas, story, sleep) and hear that while we sleep, some people work — bakers, nurses, our families on night shifts.
Materials: Bedtime sequence cards; night-worker picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Children may match their own family's real bedtime order instead of the card order.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Make and extend star patterns and count stars to 10.
Activity: Children will string star beads in a pattern (gold-silver-gold), then count out 'wishing stars' onto numbered night-sky mats.
Materials: Star beads; string; night-sky number mats
Grouping: Centers — math area; child-led after demo
Support: Fat beads and a stiff lace for children developing threading control.

Creative Art — Goal: Create a night sky with contrasting light shapes on dark paper.
Activity: Children will sponge white and yellow paint onto black paper for stars, add a foil moon, and sprinkle a pinch of glitter stars over wet paint (teacher manages glitter).
Materials: Black paper; sponges; white/yellow paint; foil; glitter (teacher-handled)
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Star stampers for children who want a clear star shape without sponge work.

Music / Movement — Goal: Sing the rhyme as a lullaby (soft voice) and as a march (strong voice).
Activity: We will sing 'Twinkle, Twinkle' twice: first rocking gently like a lullaby with scarves swaying, then marching tall and proud — noticing how changing our voices changes the feeling.
Materials: Scarves; recorded lullaby version
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A rocking chair spot for children who self-soothe with rocking during the lullaby.

Motor Activities — Goal: Reach, stretch, and balance like a star (five points).
Activity: Children will make star shapes with their bodies — arms and legs wide — holding for a count of five, then curling small like a 'sleeping star,' following the teacher's star cards.
Materials: Star pose cards; mats
Grouping: Large group — movement area; teacher-led
Support: Star poses done seated or lying down count fully for children with balance supports.

Technology — Goal: Explore a simple star/constellation app with a teacher.
Activity: With the teacher driving the tablet, children will view a night-sky app, find the brightest star, and see a simple constellation picture connected dot-to-dot.
Materials: Tablet with night-sky app; darkened corner
Grouping: Small groups; teacher-led
Support: Brightness lowered and session kept short for children sensitive to screens in the dark.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Observe the daytime sky and talk about where stars are in the day.
Activity: Outside, children will lie on a blanket and watch the sky, finding clouds shaped like things, feeling the sun's warmth, and hearing that the stars are still there, hiding in the bright light.
Materials: Blankets; sun hats; sky-watching spot
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A shady blanket spot for children sensitive to bright sun.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Practice wondering — asking questions about things we don't know yet.
Activity: The rhyme is one big question: 'How I wonder what you are.' We will practice wondering out loud about our classroom — 'I wonder why the plant leans... I wonder where the ants go' — and record our wonders on star cards.
Materials: Star cards; marker; wonder wall
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Wonder sentence starters ('I wonder...') on cards to read or point to.

title: Nursery Rhymes: Hickory Dickory Dock & Jack and Jill
subject: ELA / Reading
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Nursery Rhymes' thematic week (March): Hickory Dickory Dock & Jack and Jill. Focus book: Hickory Dickory Dock and Other Rhymes — — a classic illustrated collection of traditional nursery rhymes (substitute any Mother Goose collection on hand). Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Hickory Dickory Dock and Other Rhymes — — a classic illustrated collection of traditional nursery rhymes (substitute any Mother Goose collection on hand)

Language Arts — Goal: Act out two rhymes and put their events in order.
Activity: We will chant 'Hickory Dickory Dock' with a toy mouse running up our big clock, then 'Jack and Jill' with two puppets tumbling safely down a cushion hill, and children will order the picture cards for one rhyme.
Materials: Focus collection; toy clock; mouse finger puppet; Jack and Jill puppets; sequence cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A puppet to hold and move for children who learn the rhyme best by doing.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Test how objects roll down slopes of different steepness.
Activity: Children will roll balls and toy mice down ramps, making the ramp steeper and shallower, and compare which rolls fastest and farthest — just like tumbling down the hill.
Materials: Ramps; balls; toy mice; masking tape for finish lines
Grouping: Small groups — science table/floor
Support: A ramp with side rails for children whose ball keeps escaping the track.

Social Science — Goal: Learn that clocks help us know what happens next in our day.
Activity: Children will match picture cards of our day (arrive, play, lunch, nap, go home) to the big classroom clock's day-parts, and we will talk about how the mouse ran up at one o'clock.
Materials: Classroom schedule cards; demonstration clock
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Our real visual schedule used alongside, so the clock idea connects to our own day.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count clock numbers 1–12 and match numerals to a clock face.
Activity: Children will place numeral cards around a big floor clock in order, then count the mouse's trips up: one o'clock, the mouse ran up; two o'clock... up to five trips.
Materials: Big floor clock mat; numeral cards 1–12; toy mouse
Grouping: Large group then centers — rug/math area
Support: A completed clock picture to check against while building the floor clock.

Creative Art — Goal: Build a clock face with a moveable hand.
Activity: Children will stamp or write numerals around a paper-plate clock (with a numeral guide), attach a paper hand with a brad (teacher helps), and draw a mouse climbing the side.
Materials: Paper plates; numeral stamps; brads; markers
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Numerals pre-stamped faintly to trace for children working on numeral formation.

Music / Movement — Goal: Chant with a tick-tock beat using body percussion.
Activity: We will keep a clock beat — knees pat 'tick,' shoulders 'tock' — while chanting the rhyme, speeding the clock up and slowing it down like the teacher's metronome hand.
Materials: Teacher-led beat; tempo hands signal
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A single movement (just knees) for children who find two alternating motions tricky.

Motor Activities — Goal: Carry water carefully without spilling (crowns stay dry!).
Activity: Children will carry a small cup of water across a balance path to fill the class 'well' (a bucket), practicing slow steps — Jack and Jill's job, done carefully.
Materials: Small cups; water; balance path tape; bucket
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A half-full cup and a lid option for children building carrying control.

Technology — Goal: Use a voice recorder to hear ourselves chant and check the rhythm.
Activity: Small groups will record themselves chanting 'Hickory Dickory Dock' on the voice recorder, listen back, and decide together whether the beat stayed steady.
Materials: Voice recorder or tablet; quiet corner
Grouping: Small groups; teacher-guided
Support: Recording with a partner so no child has to perform alone.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Roll and tumble safely on a grassy slope.
Activity: Outside on our gentle grass hill, children will roll sideways down the slope one at a time, walk back up, and compare rolling on grass to rolling on the flat ground — slow and soft wins.
Materials: Grassy slope; cones for lanes
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-supervised
Support: A flat-ground forward-roll mat option for children who shouldn't use the slope.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn to take care with our bodies and to help a friend who tumbles.
Activity: Jack fell down and Jill came tumbling after — we will talk about what to do when we or a friend falls: stop, check, get a grown-up, and be gentle; children will practice offering a hand and kind words.
Materials: Feelings chart; helper picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Role-play with dolls first for children who want to practice before acting it themselves.

title: Nursery Rhymes: Rhyme Celebration Day
subject: ELA / Reading
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Nursery Rhymes' thematic week (March): Rhyme Celebration Day. Focus book: Mary Engelbreit's Mother Goose — Mary Engelbreit (classic rhymes collection). Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Mary Engelbreit's Mother Goose — Mary Engelbreit (classic rhymes collection)

Language Arts — Goal: Choose a favorite rhyme and recite its first lines with expression.
Activity: Children will pick their favorite rhyme of the week from our rhyme wall, practice it with a partner using our puppets and props, and perform the opening lines for the class celebration.
Materials: Rhyme wall cards; puppets and props from the week
Grouping: Pairs then large group — carpet
Support: Performing in a pair or with a puppet voice for children not ready to recite alone.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Review the week's investigations and share what we found out.
Activity: We will revisit our three science moments — the egg drop, the washing spout, and the rolling ramps — look at our charts, and each child will point to the result they remember best and say why.
Materials: Week science charts; ramp and ball for one more roll
Grouping: Large group — carpet/science table; teacher-led
Support: Picture results to point to for children who need a memory anchor.

Social Science — Goal: Be a kind audience and a brave performer.
Activity: We will set up a small 'stage' with a curtain cloth; children will take turns performing a rhyme and practice audience jobs: eyes watching, hands quiet, clapping at the end.
Materials: Curtain cloth; stage tape on floor; chairs
Grouping: Whole class — classroom; teacher facilitates
Support: Ticket-taker and curtain-holder jobs for children who prefer backstage roles today.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Vote and graph our favorite rhymes.
Activity: Children will place a star sticker over their favorite rhyme on our graph (Humpty, Spider, Twinkle, Hickory, Jack and Jill), then count each column and find the class winner.
Materials: Picture graph; star stickers
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Counting columns with a partner, pointing to each sticker.

Creative Art — Goal: Illustrate a favorite rhyme scene for our class book.
Activity: Each child will draw and color one scene from their favorite rhyme — the wall, the spout, the star, the clock, the hill — and dictate a caption; pages will be bound into our class Mother Goose book.
Materials: Drawing paper; crayons; markers; binding rings
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Stickers and stamps of the rhyme characters to add for children who want a starting image.

Music / Movement — Goal: Perform the week's rhymes with motions in a mini-concert.
Activity: We will sing and move through all five rhymes in order as our concert: freeze at Humpty's fall, climb with the spider, sway for Twinkle, tick-tock for Hickory, and tumble-roll for Jack and Jill.
Materials: Week props; open rug space
Grouping: Large group; teacher-led
Support: A front-corner spot with a clear view of the teacher's cue cards.

Motor Activities — Goal: Move through a rhyme obstacle course combining the week's skills.
Activity: Children will travel the course: carry an egg on a spoon, step up the 'spout' path, march around the clock circle, pour at the well, and finish twinkling like a star on the mat.
Materials: Spoons and plastic eggs; floor clock; cup and bucket; star mat
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: Stations can be skipped or shortened; extra time with no timing.

Technology — Goal: Watch our recorded rhymes and hear how we sound together.
Activity: We will listen to and watch the week's recordings of ourselves chanting, noticing how our voices and rhythm improved, and record one final class performance of our graph-winning rhyme.
Materials: Tablet with week recordings; speaker
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Volume set low and a warning before playback for sound-sensitive children.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Celebrate with a rhyme parade outdoors.
Activity: Carrying our rhyme props (star wands, mouse puppet, egg shakers), we will parade around the playground chanting our winning rhyme, finishing with freeze-dance rhymes on the grass.
Materials: Rhyme props; playground; music speaker (teacher)
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: Parade-walking with a buddy for children who need a partner in transitions.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Feel the joy of learning something by heart and sharing it.
Activity: We will close by celebrating that these rhymes now live in our heads and hearts — children will share which rhyme they will teach someone at home, and the teacher will name each child's shining moment of the week.
Materials: Class Mother Goose book; feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: The option to show their class-book page instead of speaking.

title: Pets (Preschool Unit)
subject: Social Studies
description: A 5-day preschool thematic unit on Pets (March), written as an Almanac Original. Each day is a full plan — literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor, technology, outdoor learning, and a life lesson — with goals, materials, groupings, and support strategies, plus four standing centers for the week. Days: Day 1: What Is a Pet?; Day 2: Caring for Pets: Food, Water, Shelter; Day 3: Pets Come in All Kinds; Day 4: Gentle Hands, Kind Hearts; Day 5: Our Pet Parade and Show. title: Pets: What Is a Pet?
subject: Social Studies
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Pets' thematic week (March): What Is a Pet?. Focus book: Some Pets — Angela DiTerlizzi. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Some Pets — Angela DiTerlizzi

Language Arts — Goal: Learn pet vocabulary: fur, feathers, scales, paws, whiskers.
Activity: We will read the rhyming parade of pets — furry, feathery, scaly — and add pet words to our word wall, with each child naming one animal they know in real life.
Materials: Focus book; pet word cards; word wall
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Picture word cards (fur, feather, scale) for children building animal vocabulary.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Compare animal coverings: fur, feathers, and scales.
Activity: Children will examine pet-care objects and coverings up close: a feather, a piece of faux fur, a shed snake-skin picture, and a fish-scale photo, sorting them by which animal they belong to.
Materials: Feather; faux fur; animal covering photos; magnifiers
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Magnifiers with handles and a 'look only' tray for children whose hands are still learning to be gentle.

Social Science — Goal: Share about our own pets and hear about classmates' pets.
Activity: Children who have pets will share one fact about them (name, kind, favorite game) as the teacher charts our class pet survey: how many of us have dogs, cats, fish, or no pet yet.
Materials: Class pet survey chart; photos from home (optional)
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A photo or drawing option — every child's pet story can be shown, not only told.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Sort animals into pets and wild animals and count groups.
Activity: Children will sort animal picture cards into 'could be a pet / lives in the wild,' count each group, and defend one tricky card (a goldfish? a horse?) with the group.
Materials: Animal picture cards; sorting mats; number cards
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: Fewer cards (start with 6) and a partner for children building sorting stamina.

Creative Art — Goal: Draw a pet and describe its features.
Activity: Children will draw or paint the pet they have, or the pet they dream of, labeling it with a name they choose and one detail (spots, long ears, a waggy tail).
Materials: Paper; crayons; watercolor paints; brushes
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A pre-cut pet outline available for children who want to color and decorate a pet shape.

Music / Movement — Goal: Sing a pet song with verses and animal-sound solos.
Activity: We will learn a bouncing pet song ('I have a little dog' verses suggested by children for cats, fish, and birds) with a hand-clap beat and animal sound solos.
Materials: Teacher-led song; rhythm sticks
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Instrument choices include quiet shakers for children who find the full band too loud.

Motor Activities — Goal: Move like animals: crawl, pounce, hop, and freeze.
Activity: Children will move like pets along the movement path: crawl like a cat under the scarf arch, hop softly like a rabbit, and freeze for a 'treat' (a beanbag) at the mat.
Materials: Scarf arch; mats; beanbags
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: Gentle-speed lane and a sitting-and-patting option between turns for children who tire of crawling.

Technology — Goal: Watch real pets on video and describe their behavior.
Activity: We will watch short teacher-selected clips of real pets — a kitten playing, a dog fetching, a goldfish swimming — and name what each animal is doing and what it might need next.
Materials: Projector/screen; teacher-selected pet clips
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Front-row seating for children who need the screen close and clear.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Observe real animals outdoors from a respectful distance.
Activity: Outside, we will watch for neighborhood animals — birds, squirrels, and dogs walking with their people (from a respectful distance) — and check off a picture list of what we actually saw.
Materials: Picture observation lists; clipboards
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A buddy for the walk and a picture list with only three finds for children who need a shorter hunt.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Understand that caring for a pet is a promise we keep.
Activity: A pet is not a toy — it is a living friend we promise to care for. We will talk about promises we keep (feeding a pet, being gentle) and how good it feels when someone keeps a promise to us.
Materials: Feelings chart; stuffed pet
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: The option to hold a stuffed pet while sharing, for children more comfortable with a prop.

description: Preschool day plan from the 'Pets' thematic week (March): Caring for Pets: Food, Water, Shelter. Focus book: Taking Care of a Pet — — a photo nonfiction picture book about feeding, watering, and caring for a first pet (substitute any pet-care title on hand). Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Taking Care of a Pet — — a photo nonfiction picture book about feeding, watering, and caring for a first pet (substitute any pet-care title on hand)

Language Arts — Goal: List what a pet needs every day and put care steps in order.
Activity: After reading, we will make a 'Pet Care Recipe' chart — food, water, a safe place, play, and love — and children will put the steps in a sensible morning order for a pretend dog.
Materials: Focus book; care picture cards; chart paper
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Sequencing cards with pictures for children retelling the care steps in order.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Test which materials make the best shelter from rain.
Activity: Children will test shelter materials over a paper pet — a leaf, a cloth, a box lid, plain paper — sprinkling 'rain' from a spray bottle to see which roof keeps the pet driest, learning what shelter really does.
Materials: Paper pet figures; shelter materials; spray bottle; tray
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Adult holds the 'heavy rain' bottle for children while they observe the shelter results.

Social Science — Goal: Share pet-care jobs fairly in a pretend family.
Activity: We will divide the jobs of pet care among a pretend family — who feeds, who walks, who cleans, who plays — and act the morning routine out in the home corner with the stuffed dog.
Materials: Job picture cards; stuffed dog; home corner props
Grouping: Centers — dramatic play; teacher-guided entry
Support: Picture job cards to choose from (feeder, walker, cleaner) for children deciding with visuals.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Measure and count scoops to fill amounts (more, fewer).
Activity: Children will measure pretend kibble (large dry beans) into pet bowls with scoops — two scoops for the puppy bowl, four for the big dog bowl — counting scoops aloud and comparing amounts.
Materials: Dry beans; scoops; pet bowls in two sizes; number cards
Grouping: Small group — math/practical life center
Support: A measuring cup with a fill line marked for children learning to watch the level.

Creative Art — Goal: Build a model pet home with a bed and a door.
Activity: Children will construct a pet home from a shoebox — a bed inside, a door flap, a name sign on top — for a stuffed pet to 'live' in during centers.
Materials: Shoeboxes; fabric scraps; paper; glue; crayons
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Glue sponges and larger paper shapes for children building construction skills.

Music / Movement — Goal: Perform care actions in rhythm with a song.
Activity: We will sing a 'feed the pets' action song — scooping, pouring, brushing motions for each verse's animal — ending with a gentle 'sleep, little pet' lullaby verse and quiet hands.
Materials: Teacher-led song; pretend scoop and brush props
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A spot near the teacher to watch her watering-can arm cues.

Motor Activities — Goal: Brush, clip, and walk — pet care fine and gross motor practice.
Activity: At the pet care station, children will brush stuffed animals with long strokes, clip leashes onto collars, and 'walk' their pets slowly around the rug, stopping at the water bowl mat.
Materials: Stuffed animals; brushes; clip leashes; water bowl mat
Grouping: Centers — dramatic play extension
Support: An easy-grip brush and a large stuffed dog for children building hand control.

Technology — Goal: Demonstrate a care step for a class how-to video.
Activity: Children will record a 30-second 'pet care tip' video (teacher-filmed) showing one care step with a stuffed animal, and we will watch the tips together like a class pet-care show.
Materials: Class tablet (teacher-filmed); stuffed animals
Grouping: Small groups; teacher-guided
Support: Teacher starts and stops the recording; children simply care for the pet on camera.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Care for outdoor animal visitors: water for birds and plants.
Activity: Outside, children will become caretakers of the garden corner: filling the birdbath (with teacher help), watering planters, and checking that our outdoor space is safe and welcoming for visiting animals.
Materials: Watering cans; birdbath; planters
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-supervised
Support: Partner pairs share one sprinkler cup so turns and carrying are shared.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn that responsibility means remembering what others need.
Activity: Caring is something we do every day, not only when it is fun. We will start our own class job — keeping the pretend pet center's water bowl 'full' — and talk about how the pet depends on us remembering.
Materials: Pretend pet center props; class jobs chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A shorter responsibility (the water bowl image card) to carry for children starting with one step.

title: Pets: Pets Come in All Kinds
subject: Social Studies
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Pets' thematic week (March): Pets Come in All Kinds. Focus book: What Pet Should I Get? — Dr. Seuss. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: What Pet Should I Get? — Dr. Seuss

Language Arts — Goal: Give a reason for a choice using 'because.'
Activity: We will read the rhyming dilemma of choosing one pet, pausing at each animal to name its good points, then children will complete the sentence 'I would choose a ___ because ___.'
Materials: Focus book; sentence frame cards; pet pictures
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Two picture choice cards (then three) for children building decision language gradually.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Match animals to how they move and where they live.
Activity: Children will compare how animals move and live using our covering samples and picture sets — which pets swim, fly, walk, or slither — and build a class 'pet habitat match' board.
Materials: Covering samples; habitat picture board; animal cards
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Feather and fur samples in a touch tray with picture labels for children exploring by touch first.

Social Science — Goal: Understand families choose pets that fit their homes and lives.
Activity: Families choose different pets for different lives — apartments, allergies, time (mentioned simply and kindly). Children will share (photo, drawing, or words) one reason their family's pet — or dream pet — fits their home.
Materials: Pet photos/drawings from home (optional); chart paper
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Children bring a drawing instead of a photo if their family prefers — explained kindly by the teacher.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Graph favorite pet choices and compare amounts.
Activity: After our book vote, children will graph the class's favorite pet choices from the story (dog, cat, bird, fish, and one wild-card) with name cards, counting columns and announcing the winner.
Materials: Pocket chart graph; name cards; pet picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A simple two-column graph for children new to comparing counts.

Creative Art — Goal: Use textures to show feathers, fur, or scales in art.
Activity: Children will make texture pets: cutting or tearing paper fur, gluing cotton feathers, or dotting scale patterns onto animal shapes, matching the texture to their animal.
Materials: Animal shapes; paper scraps; cotton; glue; crayons
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A torn-paper option for children who prefer tearing to cutting fur shapes.

Music / Movement — Goal: Identify animals by sound and respond with movement.
Activity: We will play 'Guess That Pet': the teacher plays an animal sound, children freeze, name the animal, and move like it for eight counts before the next sound.
Materials: Animal sound recordings; open rug
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Animal sound buttons on a choice board for children joining by pressing instead of vocalizing.

Motor Activities — Goal: Imitate varied animal movements at rotating stations.
Activity: Children will try an animal movement medley: slither like a snake on mats, flutter like a bird with scarves, swim like a fish with arm strokes, and gallop like a pony — changing at each station bell.
Materials: Mats; scarves; station bells; picture signs
Grouping: Small groups — gym area; teacher-supervised
Support: A 'slow lane' drawn beside the fast course for children moving at their own pace.

Technology — Goal: Explore a pet sound app and match sounds to animals.
Activity: At the listening/tablet center, children will tap animal pictures to hear their sounds and names in a teacher-selected pet app, matching the sound to the picture card in their hand.
Materials: Tablet with teacher-selected app; animal picture cards
Grouping: Centers — pairs; child-led after setup
Support: Headphones and a two-animal choice page for children who need fewer options.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Listen for animal sounds in our outdoor environment.
Activity: On a listening walk, children will keep silent for one minute at the garden and the playground, then list every animal sound they heard (birds, bugs, a far dog) on our outdoor sounds chart.
Materials: Outdoor sounds chart; clipboards
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A listening buddy and a two-sound checklist for children who focus best with less on the list.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn that good choices think about others' needs, not only our wants.
Activity: Choosing is hard when we want everything. We will talk about how the children in the story must pick one — and how thinking about what an animal needs helps us choose kindly and well.
Materials: Focus book; feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: The teacher models her own example first for children who need a pattern to follow.

title: Pets: Gentle Hands, Kind Hearts
subject: Social Studies
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Pets' thematic week (March): Gentle Hands, Kind Hearts. Focus book: The Perfect Pet — Margie Palatini. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: The Perfect Pet — Margie Palatini

Language Arts — Goal: Learn and use gentle-care vocabulary.
Activity: We will read about a girl whose very unusual pet turns out perfect, then brainstorm gentle-words — soft, slow, quiet, kind — and practice saying each pet rule in a gentle voice: 'Soft hands. Slow moves.'
Materials: Focus book; gentle words chart; markers
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A word bank (soft, slow, quiet, kind) to choose describing words from.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Learn to read common animal body signals.
Activity: Children will study pictures of animal faces and bodies to learn signals: ears up, ears back, tail wagging, hiding under a blanket — and sort 'I feel okay' from 'Give me space' cards, because respecting signals is part of science and kindness.
Materials: Animal signal picture cards; sorting mat
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Picture comparison cards for children sorting by feature instead of by name.

Social Science — Goal: Pretend-play a gentle vet visit with kind words.
Activity: In the vet office, children will practice a gentle check-up script — 'Hello, I will be soft. Let me listen to your heart' — taking turns as vet, assistant, and pet owner with stuffed patients.
Materials: Toy vet kit; stuffed animals; check-up cards
Grouping: Centers — dramatic play
Support: Role cards with a picture and one line to say for children who need a script.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count in pairs (sets of 2) up to 10.
Activity: Children will count pet pairs — two ears, two eyes, pairs of paws on picture animals (two front, two back) — and stamp the matching number of paw prints on counting cards.
Materials: Animal counting cards; paw print stamps; ink pads
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: Counting pairs with a partner and a number line to confirm totals.

Creative Art — Goal: Paint a calm animal portrait with watercolors.
Activity: Children will paint 'gentle pet portraits' — big soft watercolor washes for a calm animal face, adding features slowly with a thin brush when the wash dries (teacher manages drying time across the day).
Materials: Watercolor sets; thick paper; brushes; water cups
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A roller brush available for children who like painting with whole-arm movements.

Music / Movement — Goal: Sing softly and move gently to a lullaby.
Activity: We will sing a soft lullaby pet song with rocking motions, keeping voices at 'petting volume,' then tiptoe a lullaby parade around the sleeping stuffed animals.
Materials: Teacher-led song; recorded lullaby; stuffed animals
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A cushion at the circle's edge for children who enjoy the song more calmly from a seat.

Motor Activities — Goal: Move slowly with control while carrying something precious.
Activity: Children will practice slow, careful carrying: walking a 'sleeping kitten' (a soft toy on a pillow) across the room without waking it, returning along the wiggly line at a snail's pace.
Materials: Pillows; soft toy kittens; floor line
Grouping: Pairs — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A larger pom-pom 'mouse' and a shorter scooping distance for children building aim.

Technology — Goal: Observe a real vet's gentle care on video.
Activity: Children will watch a short teacher-selected video of a real veterinarian gently examining a dog, pausing to point out each gentle thing the vet does that we practiced.
Materials: Projector/screen; teacher-selected vet clip
Grouping: Small group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Teacher pre-loads one video; children press play and pause themselves.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Practice quiet, patient watching so animals feel safe.
Activity: Outside we will practice being quiet wildlife watchers: sitting at our watching spot for two minutes to let birds and bugs forget we are there, then reporting what came close.
Materials: Watching spot markers; nature journals
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: An adult stands at the watching spot with children who need reminders about distance.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Practice gentle touch and reading an animal's signals.
Activity: This is our kindest day: we will practice the two-finger petting stroke on stuffed animals (the way we would touch a real small animal), talk about reading an animal's body — happy tail, hiding, sleeping — and promise gentle hands.
Materials: Stuffed animals; animal feelings picture cards
Grouping: Large group then pairs — carpet
Support: A stuffed animal to practice on with teacher coaching before trying with a buddy.
