title: Rain, Clouds, and Wind: Clouds in the Sky
subject: Science
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Rain, Clouds, and Wind' thematic week (April): Clouds in the Sky. Focus book: It Looked Like Spilt Milk — Charles G. Shaw. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: It Looked Like Spilt Milk — Charles G. Shaw

Language Arts — Goal: Join a repetitive text pattern and guess what a shape could be.
Activity: We will read the focus book's guessing game, calling out each page's guess, and play with the pattern: 'It looked like a rabbit, but it wasn't a rabbit...' until the surprise ending tells us what it was all along.
Materials: Focus book; cloud shape cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Sentence frame ('It looked like... but it wasn't') written on the chart to join in with.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Investigate how clouds hold water until they are full, then release rain.
Activity: Our cloud experiment: children will hold a cotton-ball cloud over a cup and add water drop by drop until the cloud gets too heavy and 'rains' — counting drops before the first drip falls.
Materials: Cotton balls; droppers; cups of water; clear cups
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Pre-wrung cotton for children who just want to watch the first drips up close.

Social Science — Goal: Describe today's sky and post a group weather observation.
Activity: Children will become sky reporters: looking out our window, each small group picks today's cloud description — puffy, flat, dark, wispy, or none — and posts it on the weather station with a drawing.
Materials: Weather station board; cloud word cards; drawing supplies
Grouping: Small groups — window area
Support: Weather drawing choices (sun, cloud, rain, snow) offered as picture cards to pick from for the forecast.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Match cloud shapes to picture shapes and tally class votes.
Activity: Children will hold their cloud paintings up to shape cards — bird, rabbit, ice-cream cone, tree — voting on the class's best guesses and tallying which shape we 'saw' most often.
Materials: Cloud paintings (Day 2 art); shape cards; tally chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: White paper shapes matched to the cloud by outline for children starting with matching before naming.

Creative Art — Goal: Make symmetrical cloud prints and imagine what they look like.
Activity: Children will fold paper with a white paint blob inside, press and open it to make a symmetrical cloud, then tell the class what their cloud looks like.
Materials: White paint; blue paper; story book pictures for ideas
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Thick-handled brushes and sponges for the white paint blotting.

Music / Movement — Goal: Drift, gather, and scatter like clouds to musical cues.
Activity: We will move with our scarves as clouds: drift slowly in calm air, gather and bunch when the wind pushes, and scatter when the teacher claps thunder — always floating back together.
Materials: Scarves; recorded music; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A lap-drum option for children participating from a chair.

Motor Activities — Goal: Blow and steer 'clouds' along a path with breath control.
Activity: Children will blow cotton-ball 'clouds' across a table race track with straws (or by fanning with hands for children who shouldn't use straws), steering around the tape mountains.
Materials: Cotton balls; straws (optional per child); tape track on table
Grouping: Centers — small groups at tables
Support: A heavier cotton 'cloud' (two balls taped) for children who need more to hold.

Technology — Goal: Watch clouds move and change in a teacher-selected time-lapse.
Activity: With a teacher, children will view a slow time-lapse video of clouds crossing the sky and forming, noticing how clouds grow, stretch, and disappear like our folded paintings in motion.
Materials: Tablet or projector; teacher-selected clip
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A teacher-led single viewing for the class instead of repeated close-up tries for sensitive eyes.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Observe, draw, and describe real clouds outdoors.
Activity: Children will lie on blankets and watch real clouds move, pointing out shapes, noticing they change as they go, and choosing one cloud to draw before it drifts away.
Materials: Blankets; clipboards; paper; crayons
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A shady blanket spot and a pillow for comfortable sky watching.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Appreciate different viewpoints — two friends, two cloud pictures.
Activity: Clouds teach us that looking carefully and imagining are both valuable — we will practice seeing the same cloud two ways, learning that friends may see different things and both can be right.
Materials: Focus book; cloud paintings
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A partner to imagine with, so quieter children still get a turn to create.

title: Rain, Clouds, and Wind: Wind at Work
subject: Science
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Rain, Clouds, and Wind' thematic week (April): Wind at Work. Focus book: The Kite That Wouldn't Fly — A Windy Day Story — — a simple picture book about a kite, a gusty day, and not giving up (substitute any kite or windy-day title on hand). Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: The Kite That Wouldn't Fly — A Windy Day Story — — a simple picture book about a kite, a gusty day, and not giving up (substitute any kite or windy-day title on hand)

Language Arts — Goal: Describe what wind can do, contributing ideas to a class text.
Activity: We will read the focus book and follow the kite's ups and downs, then write a class sentence chain outside: 'The wind can...' adding each child's idea — blow leaves, push clouds, fly kites, bend grass.
Materials: Focus book; chart paper; marker
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Wind word cards with pictures (blow, gust, swirl, lift) to use in their sentence.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Test which objects wind moves best (shape and weight matter).
Activity: Using the teacher-controlled fan and safety screen, children will test paper objects — flat sheet, folded plane, tissue, card — and chart which the wind carries farthest and which it can't lift.
Materials: Fan (teacher-controlled, screened); paper test objects; measuring tape; chart
Grouping: Small groups — science table; teacher-led demo
Support: The fan stays behind its safety screen; children direct but only the teacher adjusts it.

Social Science — Goal: Learn how people use tools (flags, windsocks) to read the wind.
Activity: Children will learn why flags and windsocks exist — they show wind direction for pilots, sailors, and farmers — then hang our class windsock and check which way it points at morning and afternoon.
Materials: Class windsock; direction arrows; picture cards
Grouping: Large group — near the window/door; teacher-led
Support: A picture flag to copy for children who want an exact model to follow.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Observe and rate wind strength using visible clues.
Activity: Children will rate today's wind on our three-point wind scale using the trees outside as clues (still leaves, moving leaves, bending branches), then count and compare the week's wind ratings so far.
Materials: Wind scale chart; window/tree view; markers
Grouping: Large group — carpet/window; teacher-led
Support: A wind scale poster with faces (calm, breezy, gusty) for children rating by feel first.

Creative Art — Goal: Construct a simple kite with tail and decorations.
Activity: Children will build simple diamond kites from paper, decorating them boldly, adding tissue tails and a string handle (teacher assembles the final bridle; kites fly outdoors on Day 5 if weather allows).
Materials: Paper diamonds; tissue strips; string; crayons; tape
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Streamers stapled by a partner or teacher for children still gaining stapler-free fastening (we use tape and clips).

Music / Movement — Goal: Match movement energy to music dynamics (wind dance).
Activity: We will dance like leaves in the wind to music that swells and fades: swirl, float, gust-spin, and settle, learning to match movement size to music size.
Materials: Recorded music; scarves; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Seated scarf dancing for children participating from a chair or mat.

Motor Activities — Goal: Run and walk with streamers, feeling how speed changes them.
Activity: Children will run streamer runs across the movement space: fast runs make the streamer fly straight, slow walks let it droop — feeling wind speed with their whole bodies.
Materials: Streamer wands; open space; cones
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A streamer wand taped to the wrist for children who struggle to grip while running.

Technology — Goal: Record and review video of wind in action.
Activity: Children will take a short video with the tablet of our windsock and ribbon wands in action, then watch it in slow motion to really see the wind's pushes.
Materials: Class tablet; windsock; projector
Grouping: Small groups; teacher-guided
Support: One clear job per child (hold, aim, tap) for children who need a defined role with devices.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Detect wind direction and strength in different outdoor spots.
Activity: Children will carry ribbon wands and bubbles outside to find the wind: which way does it blow, where is it strongest (open field) and weakest (by the wall), marking discoveries on our playground map.
Materials: Ribbon wands; bubbles; playground map on clipboard
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors, in small groups
Support: A ribbons-on-a-stick wind wand for every child so no one waits for a turn to feel the wind.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Practice persistence when a project doesn't work the first time.
Activity: The kite in our story keeps falling before it flies — we will talk about how learning takes tries, and practice saying 'I'll try again' while we build today's kites together.
Materials: Focus book; kite supplies
Grouping: Large group then art center; teacher-led
Support: A paper scrap kite to practice with at the table for children frustrated by the big build.

title: Rain, Clouds, and Wind: Storms and Staying Safe
subject: Science
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Rain, Clouds, and Wind' thematic week (April): Storms and Staying Safe. Focus book: Just a Thunderstorm — Mercer Mayer. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Just a Thunderstorm — Mercer Mayer

Language Arts — Goal: Discuss a character's feelings and how he copes with a storm.
Activity: We will read about Little Critter's stormy night, talk about what scared him and what helped, and share what our families do when thunder comes.
Materials: Focus book; feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Feelings cards ready before reading so children can show, not just say, how the character feels.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Model how rain falls when a cloud is full.
Activity: Children will make mini rain clouds over cups: shaving-cream cloud on water in a clear cup, then drip colored 'rain' on top and watch it fall through when the cloud is full (teacher sets up; this is a model, and we say what real clouds do differently).
Materials: Clear cups; water; shaving cream; colored water; droppers
Grouping: Small groups — science table; teacher-guided
Support: A prediction mat with two picture options to keep guessing low-pressure.

Social Science — Goal: Pretend-play our storm safety plan with calm helper roles.
Activity: We will act out our thunderstorm plan in the cozy corner: one child is the grown-up who checks the 'weather radio,' others gather blankets and a stuffed friend, and we practice staying calm and together until the all-clear.
Materials: Prop weather radio; blankets; flashlights; stuffed animals
Grouping: Centers — dramatic play; teacher models first
Support: A helper job card with the exact words to say for children who need the script.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count seconds between 'lightning' and 'thunder' in a pretend game.
Activity: Children will practice the flash-to-thunder counting game in story form: teacher flashes a light card, we count 'one-Mississippi...' until the boom card, learning that more counts mean a farther storm.
Materials: Lightning/thunder picture cards; counting chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Start with counting to three for children building comfort with the thunder game.

Creative Art — Goal: Create a storm picture with dark colors and shiny lightning.
Activity: Children will paint a storm sky with dark blues and grays, add cotton-ball thunderclouds, and glue foil lightning bolts zig-zagging down — bold weather art for our wall.
Materials: Dark paper; blue/gray paint; cotton balls; foil strips; glue
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Glue spread with a brush instead of fingers for texture-sensitive children.

Music / Movement — Goal: Perform a group rainstorm with roles and a conductor.
Activity: We will perform our body-percussion rainstorm from Day 1 with jobs: rain patterers, wind whooshers, thunder stompers, and one lightning conductor who starts and calms the storm.
Materials: Conductor baton prop; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Movement choices offered (stomp or clap) for children who choose how to join in.

Motor Activities — Goal: Practice our severe-weather safety positions calmly.
Activity: Children will move through our storm drill relay indoors: hear the 'tornado siren' card, walk quickly to the hallway-safe wall, sit low with hands over head for a count of ten, then return when the all-clear card shows.
Materials: Cue cards (siren, all-clear); hallway practice space
Grouping: Small groups — hallway; teacher-led
Support: A walking (not running) version of each relay leg for children building speed control.

Technology — Goal: Recognize weather-alert sounds and what they tell us to do.
Activity: We will listen to real storm sounds at gentle volume and to a recorded weather-alert tone (soft), learning what the alert sound means and that it is information, not something to fear.
Materials: Listening equipment; teacher-selected gentle recordings
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: The teacher keeps volume low and pauses often; no sudden loud clips today.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Identify safe places and storm clues around our school.
Activity: If today's weather is calm, children will do a safety walk: find our building's safe door, look at where water runs in the gutters, and notice trees and the flag — talking about why we never play outside in a storm.
Materials: School grounds route; safety picture cards
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: Children who are anxious about storms walk right beside the teacher for the whole check.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Learn storm safety rules and that grown-ups help keep us safe.
Activity: We will learn our storm safety promise together: go inside, stay away from windows, let grown-ups watch the sky, and find a cozy job — then practice the promise with our classroom cozy corner setup.
Materials: Feelings chart; cozy corner items
Grouping: Large group — carpet then cozy corner
Support: A storm-comfort kit (stuffed animal, blanket) in the cozy corner for children who feel anxious today.

Language Arts — Goal: Retell a story and describe how something changes (big to small).

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Preferential seating near the book for children who need to see the fold-out pages up close.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Sort activities and pictures into day and night.

Materials: Flashlight; globe; day/night picture cards
Grouping: Small groups — science table; teacher-led demo
Support: A smaller set of six cards to start for children building sorting stamina.

Social Science — Goal: Recognize Earth as our home and find land and water on a globe.
Activity: We will spin the globe gently and find the blue water and the land, talking about how everyone we know lives on this same planet. Children will place a star sticker near where we live (teacher-guided).
Materials: Globe; star stickers
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Each child gets a turn to touch the globe with a partner nearby for support.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count stars one-to-one up to 10 and compare sizes.
Activity: Children will count felt stars onto a night-sky mat, then sort star cutouts into big, medium, and small groups and count each group.
Materials: Felt stars; night-sky mats; star cutouts
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: Star counters that stick to the mat for children whose pieces slide while counting.

Creative Art — Goal: Create a night sky using sponging and stamping.
Activity: Children will sponge deep-blue paint over black paper, then stamp stars with star sponges and add a big yellow moon circle.
Materials: Black paper; blue paint; star sponges; moon circles; smocks
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Handled sponges and a taped-down paper edge for children who need more control.

Music / Movement — Goal: Sing and move gently like twinkling stars.
Activity: We will sing 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' with hand motions, then float and twinkle around the rug to slow music, freezing as 'sleeping stars' when it stops.
Materials: Recorded gentle music; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A marked star spot to return to for children who need a home base during movement.

Motor Activities — Goal: Develop aim and arm strength tossing underhand.
Activity: Children will toss soft beanbag 'moon rocks' into crater hoops on the floor, stepping back one floor star at a time as they succeed.

Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A closer starting line and larger hoops for children building aim.

Technology — Goal: View the night sky through a teacher-led projection.
Activity: We will dim the lights and watch a projected star field (teacher-selected planetarium app) while the teacher names a few bright stars and the children find the biggest one.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A warning before the lights dim and a seat near the teacher for children uneasy in the dark.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Observe shadows and how the sun makes them.

Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A partner to stand with for the tracing game and a hat reminder for sun safety.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Picture prompts (moon, stars, rocket) for children choosing a wonder.

Activity: Children will build patterns with crescent and full-moon cards (full, crescent, full, crescent) and read their pattern aloud, then try a three-shape pattern.
Materials: Moon shape cards; pattern strips
Grouping: Centers — math area; child-led after demo
Support: Starter strips with the first two shapes placed for children new to patterning.

Creative Art — Goal: Print textures to represent the moon's surface.

Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Foil balls with a larger grip size and pre-drawn moon circles.

Music / Movement — Goal: Move slowly and with control like astronauts on the moon.

Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A shorter path across the rug and a partner moving alongside.

Motor Activities — Goal: Develop balance walking heel-to-toe on a line.
Activity: Children will moon-walk along a taped curving path, arms out for balance, collecting a moon rock (beanbag) at the end to bring back to the 'lander.'

Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A wider tape path and a teacher's hand available for children still developing balance.

Grouping: Centers — pairs; child-led after setup
Support: A page-number bookmark and volume set by the teacher.

Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A shaded sitting spot and a clipboard with a pencil strap for easier handling.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Specific praise for children who describe waiting in their own words.

Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A smaller jump (heels-up bounce) option and a clear floor spot for safety.

Support: Specific praise that names the child's effort when they share.

Language Arts — Goal: Name the planets and match name cards to pictures.
Activity: We will read the rhyming tour of the planets, then play a matching game: children hold planet picture cards and find the matching name/picture on our solar system chart as the teacher reads clues.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Planet cards color-coded to match the chart for children who need a visual cue.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Compare planets by size (big and small) using models.
Activity: Using balls of different sizes, we will compare the giant sun ball to planet balls, order our classroom planets from biggest to smallest, and feel how heavy 'Jupiter' is next to tiny 'Mercury.'
Materials: Assorted balls; planet labels; balance scale
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Only three planets (biggest, middle, smallest) for children starting with simple comparisons.

Social Science — Goal: Understand Earth is the planet where people live and why it is special.
Activity: We will talk about what makes Earth just right for us — air, water, and warmth — and look at our globe again to find the land and oceans where people and animals live.
Materials: Globe; focus book
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Turn-and-talk with a partner before whole-group answers.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Use ordinal numbers: first, second, third in a sequence.
Activity: Children will place planet cards in order on a long strip starting from the sun, saying 'Mercury is first, Venus is second...' as far as they can, with the class completing the line together.
Materials: Planet cards; long order strip; sun starter card
Grouping: Small group — math center; teacher-guided
Support: A completed mini-chart to copy for children who need a model.

Creative Art — Goal: Create a planet using marble-painting technique.
Activity: Children will drip paint onto paper inside a tray and roll marbles through it to swirl planet colors, choosing colors for a real planet or inventing their own.
Materials: Trays; paper circles; paint; marbles; smocks
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A tray with raised edges and larger marbles for easier control.

Music / Movement — Goal: Move in a circle 'orbit' and respond to planet name cues.
Activity: We will march in an orbit around a sun mat while music plays; when the teacher calls a planet, everyone freezes in that planet's pose (spin small, stretch big, sway ringed).

Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Pose picture cards displayed during the game for children who need reminders.

Motor Activities — Goal: Practice throwing and catching with control.
Activity: Children will play 'meteor catch' with soft balls in pairs, stepping one step apart after each successful catch, then play ring toss onto planet cones.
Materials: Soft balls; rings; cones with planet pictures
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A lighter foam ball and closer distance for children building catching skills.

Technology — Goal: Explore a planet app with a teacher and make choices.
Activity: In pairs with the teacher nearby, children will tap planets on a teacher-selected tablet app to hear their names and see them spin, choosing which planet to visit next.
Materials: Tablet with teacher-selected space app

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Four symbols only on the graph for children building symbol recognition.

Support: Pre-cut strips for children who want to start gluing right away; extra glue time allowed.

Grouping: Whole class — entry area; teacher-led
Support: The teacher's own gear demonstrated first as a model for children unsure of the routine.

Activity: Using the book's snowy morning, children will sequence getting-dressed cards for a cold rainy day — under-layer, warm clothes, coat, hat, boots — and count how many layers Peter's day needed versus our spring day.
Materials: Dressing sequence cards; layer counters
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A sequencing strip to lay cards on for children who need the in-order anchor.

Creative Art — Goal: Paint rain using spray bottles (streaks and drips).
Activity: Children will paint rainy-day pictures by spraying diluted blue paint from spray bottles onto paper held at the easel (outside edge of the art area), watching the rain streak and drip.
Materials: Spray bottles; diluted washable paint; easel paper; smocks; drop cloth
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5; supervised
Support: Dot markers as a gentler-grip option for the rain painting.

Music / Movement — Goal: Build a storm with body sounds that grow and calm down.
Activity: We will move through a rainstorm with our bodies: fingers patter sprinkle, hands drum harder rain, feet stomp thunder on the teacher's count, arms wave the wind, then everything calms to sun.
Materials: Teacher-led cues; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Cue cards shown ahead of the thunder sound for children startled by sudden noises.

Motor Activities — Goal: Practice dressing skills: zipping, pulling on boots and hats.
Activity: At the dress-up relay, children will practice the real skill: pull on a jacket, zip it, put on a hat and boots, walk to the 'door' cone, and come back to undress — no racing, just practice.

Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A stool to sit on while dressing the lower half for children with balance needs.

Support: A timer visible for turn length so waiting children know exactly when their turn comes.

Support: Extra dry socks from our class stash so wet feet never spoil the learning.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A pocket on the chart for children to slip their choice card in quietly.

Materials: Focus book; poster paper; markers
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Picture prompts for children deciding which rule to teach their animal puppet.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Match animals to their natural homes (habitats).
Activity: Children will match wild animal cards to their homes — bird to nest, rabbit to burrow, fish to pond, bee to hive — and notice that every animal needs a home that fits it.
Materials: Animal and habitat cards; felt board
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: A partner to check the match with and larger cards for easier handling.

Social Science — Goal: Distinguish wild animals from pets and learn about wildlife helpers.
Activity: We will sort photos into 'wild animals' and 'pet animals,' then talk about why vets for wild animals (wildlife rehabilitators) wear gloves and let animals go back home when they are better.
Materials: Animal photo cards; sorting mats
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Partner sorting so decisions are made together.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count animals in a scene by location up to 10.
Activity: Children will count the animals in a big habitat mural photo (birds in trees, fish in the pond, rabbits in grass) and write or stamp the number they found for each home.
Materials: Habitat scene poster; stamp pads; number cards
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: A model habitat card to copy for children who need an example.

Creative Art — Goal: Sculpt a nest using natural and collage materials.
Activity: Children will build bird nests from clay, shredded paper, and sticks, pressing in three speckled playdough eggs and thinking about how birds carry every single piece.
Materials: Clay; shredded paper; sticks; playdough eggs
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Pre-formed clay base for children who need a sturdier start.

Music / Movement — Goal: Change movements to match each animal in a song.
Activity: We will play an animal-action song: hop like a rabbit, flap like a bird, scurry like a mouse, freeze like a deer — changing with each verse's animal picture.
Materials: Recorded music; animal picture cards
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A defined leaf-spot to return to between animals for children who need a base.

Motor Activities — Goal: Walk slowly and carefully carrying a fragile 'patient.'
Activity: Children will tiptoe along a 'quiet forest path' carrying an 'injured' stuffed owl in both hands to the wildlife center mat, moving slowly so they never jostle their patient.
Materials: Stuffed owl; path markers; center mat
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: Extra time and a two-step route for children building confidence.

Technology — Goal: Watch wildlife helpers and sequence what they do.
Activity: We will watch a short teacher-selected clip of a wild animal being cared for and released back to nature, then name what the helpers did in order.
Materials: Projector; teacher-selected clip
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Front seats for children who need to be close to the screen; warning before the happy release moment gets exciting.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Build a shelter home for insects in our garden.
Activity: In a corner of the garden we will build an insect hotel: stacking sticks, pinecones, and bark pieces (all teacher-checked) into a box, then step back and watch to see if anyone moves in.
Materials: Wooden box; sticks; pinecones; bark (teacher-collected)
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: Jobs offered (holder, layer, watcher) so children can join at their comfort level.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Show respect for wildlife by observing without disturbing.
Activity: We will talk about respecting wild things — watching a bird from far away is loving it in the way it needs. Children will share one wild animal they promise to watch gently.
Materials: Feelings chart; animal photos
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Sentence frame ('I respect ___ because...') for support.

evidence:

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Tally and count events with one-to-one marks.
Activity: As our adoption fair runs, we will tally each adoption on a chart, count the total at the end, and celebrate that every animal found a match.

Grouping: Large group — classroom; teacher-led

Creative Art — Goal: Create decorations for a shared celebration.
Activity: Children will decorate our 'Adoption Day' banner and finish the shelter with drawings of happy families walking their new pets.

Grouping: Large group in shifts — art area
Support: Banner letters pre-outlined for children to fill with color.

Music / Movement — Goal: Perform favorite songs for an audience.
Activity: We will perform our week's animal songs — the check-up song and the animal-action song — for our guests at the fair (or a neighboring class), with big actions and bows.

Grouping: Large group; teacher-led
Support: A front-line spot with a clear view of the teacher's actions for cueing.

Motor Activities — Goal: Complete a celebration parade course with a carried 'pet.'
Activity: Children and their newly 'adopted' stuffed animals will complete a parade course: heel-walk the line, step over the 'puddles,' spin once at the park cone, and cross the finish line together.
Materials: Floor path; cones; stuffed animals
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: Choice of two course paths (shorter/longer) at the start.

Technology — Goal: Watch and discuss photos documenting our week.
Activity: We will watch our Animal Rescue slideshow — the vet clinic, bed-testing, our shelter, and insect hotel — and each child will spot one photo they are in and tell what we were doing.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Front seating for screen viewing; the class book offered as an alternative telling of the week.

Activity: We will hold our adoption fair outdoors on blankets: families (classmates) visit each blanket shelter, meet the animals, read their signs, and 'adopt' with a handshake and certificate.

Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: Blanket spots with extra shade for children who need a rest place.

Activity: We will close Animal Rescue week by talking about promises: a pet is cared for every day, not just on special days. Each child will share their promise to an animal they love or would love.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: The option to show their adoption page instead of speaking aloud.

title: Animals Around the World: African Savanna
subject: Science
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Animals Around the World' thematic week (May): African Savanna. Focus book: Giraffes Can't Dance — Giles Andreae. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Giraffes Can't Dance — Giles Andreae

Language Arts — Goal: Learn animal action words and use them in sentences.
Activity: We will read how Gerald the giraffe finds his own dance, then collect savanna action words (gallop, stomp, swish, prowl) and act out each one after we say it.
Materials: Focus book; action word cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Animal cards to hold and name for children who need a concrete prompt.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Identify the savanna habitat and the animals that live there.
Activity: Children will sort animal cards into 'lives on the savanna' and 'does not,' checking our world map poster for clues: the savanna is hot with tall grass and few trees.
Materials: Animal cards; habitat poster; sorting mats
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: A two-habitat start (savanna/not savanna with five cards) for children building sorting skill.

Social Science — Goal: Locate Africa and recognize it as a place with people and animals.
Activity: We will find Africa on the globe, notice how big it is, and talk simply about the people and animals who share its grasslands, and how far away it is from our school.
Materials: Globe; simple world map
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A tracing finger partner activity so every child gets a turn on the globe.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Compare heights and order objects tallest to shortest.
Activity: Children will build cube towers to compare animal heights — a tall giraffe tower, a medium zebra tower, a small warthog tower — and order them tallest to shortest.
Materials: Unifix cubes; animal height cards
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: Cube stacks started for children (first three cubes placed) to continue.

Creative Art — Goal: Paint a habitat scene in horizontal color bands.
Activity: Children will paint a savanna sunset with wide orange, pink, and red bands, then add a black-painted acacia tree shape and animal silhouettes when the sky dries.
Materials: Tempera paints; brushes; paper; tree shapes
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Pre-cut tree shapes and a sponge on a clothespin for children who need a grippier tool.

Music / Movement — Goal: Respond to different styles of music with different dances.
Activity: Like Gerald, we will try dancing different ways to different music — a slow swaying waltz, a bouncy tango — and vote with our feet on which music fits us best.
Materials: Recorded waltz and tango clips; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Simpler two-beat steps modeled slowly for children learning the waltz pattern.

Motor Activities — Goal: Use large body movements to imitate animal travel.
Activity: Children will practice savanna animal moves across the movement area: giraffe stretches up tall, zebra gallops, lion prowls low, and warthog trots.
Materials: Movement cards; open space
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: Step markers on the floor showing where each foot goes for the gallop.

Technology — Goal: Explore real animal photos and sounds with a teacher.
Activity: With the teacher, small groups will look at real photos of savanna animals on the tablet and listen to one real animal sound, guessing the animal before the picture is revealed.
Materials: Tablet with teacher-selected photos and sounds
Grouping: Small groups; teacher-led
Support: Teacher holds the tablet while children direct which animal to find next.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Observe sun and shade and connect to animals' needs.
Activity: On a savanna walk (our sunny field), children will feel how warm the sun is, look for grass and the shadiest tree, and talk about why savanna animals rest in the shade at midday.
Materials: Field; shade tree; clipboards
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A shady check-in spot and a water break built into the walk.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Appreciate that everyone has their own talent.
Activity: Gerald could not dance like the others — until he found his own music. We will talk about how everyone has something they are good at, and each child will name one of their talents.
Materials: Focus book (Gerald's dance page); feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Specific praise for children who name a talent, however small.

title: Animals Around the World: The Arctic
subject: Science
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Animals Around the World' thematic week (May): The Arctic. Focus book: Polar Bear, Polar Bear, What Do You Hear? — Bill Martin Jr. and Eric Carle. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Polar Bear, Polar Bear, What Do You Hear? — Bill Martin Jr. and Eric Carle

Language Arts — Goal: Join in patterned text and add animal sound words.
Activity: We will read the patterned focus book, joining in the repeated lines, and add 'hearing' words (roaring, snorting, trumpeting) to our sound-word chart.
Materials: Focus book; sound-word chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: The class joins the pattern aloud, giving every child the words to say together.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Explore ice and discover how fat (blubber) keeps arctic animals warm.
Activity: Children will explore ice cubes with their hands (cold! smooth! melting!), then watch the teacher's 'blubber glove' demo: a shortening-covered glove in ice water stays comfortable, like a polar bear's fat keeps it warm.
Materials: Ice cubes; towels; shortening glove in a bag (teacher demo); ice water bin
Grouping: Small groups — science table; teacher-led demo
Support: Front-row spot and a partner to share observations with.

Social Science — Goal: Recognize how people dress for a very cold climate.
Activity: We will find the Arctic at the top of the globe, then dress a paper person for arctic weather, choosing from clothing pictures (coat, mittens, swimsuit, sandals) and explaining each choice.
Materials: Globe; paper person; clothing picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A clothing basket to handle items rather than picture-only sorting.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count animals on 'ice floes' one-to-one up to 10.
Activity: Children will place toy polar bears and penguins onto numbered ice-floe mats, counting each animal as it steps on, then compare floes: which has more animals?
Materials: Toy bears and penguins; numbered mats
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: Pairs of mittens and counters that stay put on felt for children whose pieces slide.

Creative Art — Goal: Create a snowy scene using collage and texture.
Activity: Children will glue cotton-ball snow and torn white paper onto blue paper to build an arctic scene, then add a chalk polar bear drawn with the teacher's outline.
Materials: Blue paper; cotton balls; white paper; glue; chalk
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Large cotton balls and a glue dish to dip rather than squeeze bottles.

Music / Movement — Goal: Move smoothly and slowly in response to music.
Activity: We will slide and glide across the rug like seals and skaters to slow, sparkly music, freezing in a curled 'sleeping bear' shape when it stops.
Materials: Recorded slow music; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A personal ice-floe mat to slide on for children who need a defined space.

Motor Activities — Goal: Build balance waddling with an object on the feet.
Activity: Children will waddle like penguins across the rug holding a beanbag 'egg' on top of their feet for a few careful steps, then pass the egg to the next penguin.
Materials: Beanbags; floor markers
Grouping: Small groups — rug; teacher-supervised
Support: A very short route with a teacher walking alongside.

Technology — Goal: Identify arctic sounds at the listening center.
Activity: Children will use the listening center to hear recorded arctic wind and animal sounds, holding up the matching animal card when they recognize a sound.
Materials: Listening center; recorded sounds; animal cards
Grouping: Centers — pairs; child-led after setup
Support: Headphones and a pre-set pause point so the clip stays short.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Compare melting ice in sun and shade.
Activity: Outside, each pair will carry an ice chunk in a tray to a sunny spot and a shady spot, checking back to see which melts faster, and drawing the puddle results in journals.
Materials: Ice chunks; trays; journals; sunny and shady spots
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: Warmer ice chunks that are easier to grip, with mittens available.

Activity: We will talk simply about how the Arctic animals' icy home needs people everywhere to take care of the Earth, and one small thing our class does (not wasting, cleaning up) that helps.
Materials: Arctic photo; feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Sentence frame ('I keep ___ safe by...') for support.

title: Animals Around the World: The Ocean
subject: Science

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Animal name cards with photos to hold up at their page.

Activity: Children will examine real shells, starfish shapes, and sand with magnifiers, and test which of our ocean objects float and which sink in the water bin.

Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Magnifiers offered and a 'scientist partner' to compare findings with.

Activity: We will look at the globe and see how much of Earth is ocean, then talk about people who work on the water — fishers, lifeguards, sailors — and the boats they use.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Turn-and-talk with a partner before answering whole-group.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Sort and order shells by size and count a group.
Activity: Children will sort a shell collection by size (big/small) then by kind, count their favorite group, and line shells up in a size order from smallest to biggest.

Grouping: Centers — science/math area; child-led
Support: Sorting trays with raised edges and fewer shells per round on request.

Creative Art — Goal: Create a wax-resist ocean picture.
Activity: Children will draw fish with white crayons on white paper (hard to see!) and then paint a blue watercolor wash over the page to reveal their fish swimming.
Materials: White crayons; paper; blue watercolor; brushes
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Pre-drawn fish templates for children coloring within a shape rather than resisting freehand.

Music / Movement — Goal: Move like waves and sea creatures to flowing music.
Activity: Holding blue scarves as waves, we will move to flowing music — bobbing like boats, rippling like water, and swooping like gulls — slowing as the 'tide' (music) calms.
Materials: Blue scarves; recorded flowing music
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Scarf colors matched to a picture card for children who choose their move by color.

Motor Activities — Goal: Walk a low beam and move like sea animals with control.
Activity: Children will walk the 'plank' (low balance beam), then crab-walk sideways across the mat and 'swim' with big arm circles back to the start.
Materials: Low balance beam; mats
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A wider plank and a spotter partner for children still building confidence.

Activity: We will watch a short, teacher-selected underwater clip of real fish and turtles, pausing to count fish and name colors as they pass.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Front seating and the volume kept low with captions of the teacher's narration.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Complete an ocean-themed movement course outdoors.
Activity: Outside we will play an ocean voyage course: row (pretend) across the grass 'sea,' walk the plank line, toss a ring 'life preserver' to a partner, and dock at the cone island.

Support: A shorter plank distance and a hoop target at floor level for tossing.

Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Picture choices (pick up trash, use less plastic) for children selecting their promise.

Language Arts — Goal: Use loud and quiet voices on purpose while reading rhymes.
Activity: We will read the jungle rhymes and practice each animal's voice — the lion's roar, the snake's hiss-whisper — talking about when we use loud voices and when we use quiet ones.
Materials: Focus book; voice picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Volume picture cards (whisper/speak/roar) for children choosing how to say their line.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Place jungle animals in the layer where they live.
Activity: Using a simple layered model (floor, bushes, tall trees, treetops), children will place animal cards where each animal lives and check with the teacher why monkeys stay high and tigers prowl low.
Materials: Layer model; animal cards
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: A completed layer example standing beside them as a model.

Social Science — Goal: Locate jungles on the globe and compare climates.
Activity: We will find jungles near the middle of the globe (the warm equator band), compare jungle weather to ours, and imagine packing a bag for a jungle trip.
Materials: Globe; packing picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A pointer stick passed hand to hand so each child can lead one step of the trip.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Measure and compare lengths with cubes.
Activity: Children will measure big leaves with unifix cubes, record which leaf is longest on our class chart, and sort leaf cutouts by length.
Materials: Real and paper leaves; unifix cubes; class chart
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: Leaves arranged on a grid mat for children who need structure while measuring.

Creative Art — Goal: Collage a layered jungle with torn paper.
Activity: Children will tear and glue layers of green paper — dark at the bottom, light at the top — to make a leafy jungle, then tuck in one drawn animal hiding in the leaves.
Materials: Green papers in shades; glue; paper; crayons
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Pre-torn leaf papers and a defined gluing area for children who need boundaries.

Music / Movement — Goal: Play rhythms loud and soft following a conductor.
Activity: We will build a jungle rhythm band: drums rumble like thunder, shakers hiss like rain, and sticks click like woodpeckers, following the teacher's loud and soft signals.
Materials: Drums; shakers; rhythm sticks; signal cards
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: An instrument with a handle and a picture cue for loud/soft changes.

Motor Activities — Goal: Climb, crawl, and stomp with strength and control.
Activity: Children will move through a jungle course: stomp like elephants, slither under a low branch (limbo bar), and climb the playground climber like monkeys with a teacher spotting.
Materials: Playground climber; limbo bar; open space
Grouping: Small groups — outdoors/gym; teacher-supervised
Support: Teacher-supervised single turns on the climber, with a ground-level 'vine swing' (rope) alternative.

Technology — Goal: Record a group soundscape and identify sounds on playback.
Activity: We will record our own jungle soundscape — voices and instruments making rain, frogs, and monkey calls — then listen back and guess: what made that sound?
Materials: Voice recorder or tablet (teacher-operated); instruments
Grouping: Large group; teacher-led
Support: Children who prefer not to record can operate the start/stop with the teacher.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Search nature for leaves and shades of green.
Activity: On a jungle explorer walk around our schoolyard, children will hunt for the biggest leaves and count how many different shades of green they can find, sketching their biggest leaf.
Materials: Clipboards; journals; crayons
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A 'most greens' recording partner for children who find drawing hard — they can tally instead.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Appreciate that everyone has their own voice and style.
Activity: Every animal in the jungle has its own sound and its own way. We will talk about how each of us has a special voice too, and practice using the right voice for the right place (playground loud, library quiet).
Materials: Focus book (favorite rhyme); feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Sentence frame ('My voice is best for...') for support.

title: Animals Around the World: Australia
subject: Science
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Animals Around the World' thematic week (May): Australia. Focus book: Koala Lou — Mem Fox. Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Koala Lou — Mem Fox

Language Arts — Goal: Retell a story using new vocabulary from Australia.
Activity: We will read how Koala Lou practices for the Bush Olympics to make her mother proud, then talk about the new words (bush, joey, gum tree) and retell Lou's three events with picture cards.
Materials: Focus book; story picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Word cards for children to sequence the story with instead of speaking first.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Sort animals into daytime and nighttime (nocturnal) groups.
Activity: Children will sort animal cards into day-active and night-active (nocturnal) animals, including Australia's koalas who sleep in the day, placing them on our sun/moon chart.
Materials: Animal cards; sun/moon chart
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: A day/night pocket chart within reach for independent checking.

Social Science — Goal: Locate Australia and recognize similarities between children there and here.
Activity: We will spin the globe to find Australia — an island continent far across the ocean — and talk about how people there live in houses and go to school just like us, with different animals outside.
Materials: Globe; photos (teacher-selected)
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A 'far away' visual — a photo line from our school to the globe — for children grasping distance.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count hops to match numerals and graph a class favorite.
Activity: Children will play a kangaroo counting game: each child hops the number of times shown on a card (up to 10), and as a class we will graph our favorite animal from the whole week's travels.
Materials: Number cards; floor graph; animal picture cards
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Counting together in a bounce-along way for children who need rhythm to count.

Creative Art — Goal: Create a koala picture with handprint art.
Activity: Children will make a handprint koala (gray painted hand, fingers as the koala climbing) on a paper eucalyptus branch and add fingerprint leaves around it.
Materials: Gray paint; paper branches; green paint; smocks
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A traced hand template for children who find handprint printing difficult.

Music / Movement — Goal: Hop and freeze in response to music cues.
Activity: We will hop, bound, and stretch to bouncy Australian-flavored music, freezing inside hula-hoop 'pouches' when the music stops and peeking out like joeys.
Materials: Recorded bouncy music; hula hoops
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Freeze spots on the floor for children who need a clear landing place.

Motor Activities — Goal: Hop with two feet together while carrying an object.
Activity: Children will hop like kangaroos carrying a soft ball in an apron 'pouch' across the rug, then switch to wombat waddling back, keeping their pouch passenger safe.
Materials: Aprons with pockets; soft balls; floor markers
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A lower hoop to hop through and a walking option between hops.

Technology — Goal: Review five habitats through a photo slideshow quiz.
Activity: We will watch our Animals Around the World slideshow — the teacher's photos from each day — and call out the habitat name for each picture before the label appears.
Materials: Projector; teacher-assembled slideshow
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Front seats and a chance to hold the clicker (with teacher) for engagement.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Celebrate learning by moving like animals from all five habitats.
Activity: Our celebration parade will circle the playground: each child moves like their favorite animal from the whole week — savanna, arctic, ocean, jungle, or outback — while the class guesses who they are.
Materials: Playground; habitat picture cards
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; pairs
Support: Partner pairing with a confident fact-sharer for children still building recall.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Feel valued for who we are, not just for winning.
Activity: Koala Lou's mother loved her 'just as she was,' win or lose. We will talk about trying our best and being loved for who we are, and each child will hear one thing they did well this week.
Materials: Focus book (ending pages); feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Specific praise from the teacher naming each child's effort this week.

subject: Social Studies

evidence:
Focus book: Deserts Are Dry — — a simple nonfiction picture book introducing deserts, dunes, and dry lands (substitute any desert title on hand)

Language Arts — Goal: Learn and use desert vocabulary.
Activity: We will read the focus book and build a word wall for the desert: desert, dry, dune, sand, oasis. Children will use one new word to describe our classroom sand bin.
Materials: Focus book; word cards with photos
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Picture word cards to hold while saying the new words.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Compare building with dry sand and wet sand.
Activity: Children will try to build with dry sand, then with a little water sprinkled in, discovering that wet sand holds shapes and dry sand slips away. We will record which worked for castles.
Materials: Sand trays; spray bottles; molds
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Extra building time and a cup of water measured by the teacher for their test.

Social Science — Goal: Locate deserts on the globe and learn how people live there.
Activity: We will find the big desert bands on our globe, talk about the people who live in deserts and how they dress for the sun (hats, loose clothes, staying in shade at midday), and compare to our clothes today.
Materials: Globe; clothing picture cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A world map floor mat to walk on for children who learn by moving.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Sort by size and count objects in a scene to 10.
Activity: Children will sort desert scene cards by size (big dune, small rock, tall cactus) and count the cacti hiding in a desert picture, marking each with a clip as they count.
Materials: Desert scene cards; clothespins; picture poster
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: A simple two-group sort offered first for children beginning classification.

Creative Art — Goal: Create layered sand art by pouring with control.
Activity: Children will pour layers of colored sand through funnels into clear cups to make desert sunset stripes, choosing their color order and naming each layer.
Materials: Colored sand; funnels; clear cups; trays
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Funnels with wider spouts and a tray to catch spills for children building pouring control.

Music / Movement — Goal: Move slowly and fluidly like desert wind.
Activity: To slow, drifting music, children will sway scarves like hot wind and roll gently across the rug like tumbleweeds, freezing when the wind (music) stops.
Materials: Scarves; recorded slow music
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: A seated swaying option and slower music for children who prefer calm movement.

Motor Activities — Goal: Walk an uneven path while carrying an object with both hands.
Activity: Children will walk our dune path — up the ramp, across the wobble board 'ridge,' and down — carrying an empty 'water jug' with two hands like desert travelers.
Materials: Ramp; wobble board; light jugs; mats
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A shorter, flatter path for children who need less climbing challenge.

Technology — Goal: Compare places through guided photographs.
Activity: We will view a projected slideshow of real desert photographs (teacher-selected) and compare each to a photo of our own schoolyard: what is the same? What is missing?
Materials: Projector; teacher-selected desert photos; schoolyard photo
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A seat near the screen and the teacher's narration filling in quiet parts.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Compare sunny and shady places and explore sand outdoors.
Activity: Outside, we will find the sunniest and shadiest spots in our yard, touch the ground in each (with the teacher checking temperature safety), and visit the sandbox to build and compare sand piles in sun and shade.
Materials: Sandbox; buckets; playground sun/shade areas
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A buddy and a hat check before going out for children sensitive to heat and sun.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Feel gratitude for water in our everyday lives.
Activity: We will talk about how little water deserts have and how much we use without thinking — drinking, washing, playing. Children will name one moment they are glad to have water.
Materials: Feelings chart; water drop cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Sentence frame ('I am thankful for water when...') for support.

Language Arts — Goal: Learn desert animal names and dictate a fact.
Activity: We will read about camels, fennec foxes, owls, and lizards. Children will choose a favorite desert animal and dictate one fact sentence for our desert animal wall.

Grouping: Large group then small groups — carpet/tables
Support: Animal picture cards to hold while the class names each one.

Activity: Children will learn that many desert animals sleep all day and come out at night when it is cool. We will sort animal cards onto our sun chart and moon chart and check them against the focus book.
Materials: Animal cards; sun/moon charts
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: Only day/night sorting with six cards for children starting the idea.

Social Science — Goal: Understand respectful watching of wild desert animals.
Activity: We will talk about how desert animals live far from towns where few people are, and how visitors watch them quietly without feeding or chasing — the same gentle rules as our schoolyard animals.
Materials: Focus book photos; globe
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: 'Far away' shown with a string across the globe for children grasping distance.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Sort by a feature (humps) and count groups to 10.
Activity: Children will sort camel cards by one hump or two humps, count each group, and count the animals drinking at our felt waterhole picture one by one.
Materials: Camel cards; waterhole felt scene
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: Hump cards only (no text) for children sorting by picture alone.

Creative Art — Goal: Paint a sunset scene with silhouettes.
Activity: Children will paint a desert sunset with warm bands of color and, once dry, add camel and cactus silhouettes in dark paint along the horizon.
Materials: Tempera paints; brushes; paper
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Pre-cut camel shapes for children who want to paint the sunset first.

Music / Movement — Goal: Change movements to match animal cues in a dance game.
Activity: We will play 'desert animal freeze dance': move like the animal on the card the teacher raises while music plays, and freeze in the shade (a hoop) when it stops.
Materials: Recorded music; animal cards; hoops
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Animal picture cards flipped as cues by the teacher at a slower pace.

Motor Activities — Goal: Imitate desert animal movements with control.
Activity: Children will slither like snakes under the low bar, hop like kangaroo rats between rocks (spots), and tiptoe like a fox around the cactus cones.
Materials: Low bar; floor spots; cones
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A shorter slither distance and the choice to move on the mat instead of the floor.

Technology — Goal: Match desert night sounds to their sources.
Activity: Children will listen to recorded desert night sounds (owl hoots, wind, crickets) on the tablet and match each sound to its picture on our night board.
Materials: Tablet with teacher-selected sounds; picture board
Grouping: Small group — listening area; teacher-guided
Support: Headphones and a two-animal choice board for children who need fewer options.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Follow and identify animal tracks in sand.
Activity: In the sandbox, the teacher will press animal-track stamps into the sand; children will follow the trail like trackers, guessing which animal passed and drawing one track in their journals.

Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A partner tracker to walk with and compare prints side by side.

Materials: Animal photos; feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Sentence frame ('I am amazing because I can...') for support.

title: Desert / Egypt: Cactus and Desert Plants
subject: Social Studies
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Desert / Egypt' thematic week (May): Cactus and Desert Plants. Focus book: Plants in Dry Places — — a picture book about cacti and the plants that live in dry places (substitute any desert-plants title on hand). Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: Plants in Dry Places — — a picture book about cacti and the plants that live in dry places (substitute any desert-plants title on hand)

Language Arts — Goal: Label plant parts and describe with adjectives.
Activity: We will read the focus book and label a big cactus diagram together: flower, arm, spines, roots. Children will practice describing a cactus using two describing words (tall, prickly, green).
Materials: Focus book; cactus diagram; label cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: The label words placed on the diagram by the teacher for children to point to and name.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Compare how materials absorb and hold water.
Activity: Children will test how a cactus 'stores' water: we will soak a sponge and a paper towel, squeeze each into cups, and compare which held more water — the sponge is like the cactus's thick stem.
Materials: Sponges; paper towels; cups; water trays
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: A partner to compare sponges with and a results picture chart to mark.

Social Science — Goal: Connect a plant to the animals it helps (a simple web of life).
Activity: We will build a simple web with yarn: the cactus in the middle connects to the bird that nests in it, the bat that visits its flowers, and the animals that eat its fruit — plants help the whole desert.
Materials: Yarn; picture cards; cactus photo
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Fewer web strings (animal, shade, fruit) for children building the connection idea.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Measure heights with cubes and order by height.
Activity: Children will measure our paper cactus garden with unifix cubes, write or stamp each height, and arrange the cacti in order from shortest to tallest.
Materials: Paper cacti; unifix cubes; number stamps
Grouping: Small group — math center
Support: Three cacti only (short, medium, tall) for children starting measurement.

Creative Art — Goal: Create a cactus with handprint and fingerprint techniques.
Activity: Children will print a handprint cactus (green hand, fingers up) on paper, then add fingerprint 'spines' and a tissue-paper flower blooming on top.
Materials: Green paint; paper; tissue flowers; smocks
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Spine dots made with a fingertip instead of tools for children who prefer direct touch (washed hands after).

Music / Movement — Goal: Grow through a slow movement sequence like a plant.
Activity: To calm music, we will 'grow' like a cactus: start as a tiny seed, sprout one arm, then the other, and finally bloom — opening our hands like flowers on the last note.
Materials: Recorded calm music; open space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Movements from a seated position offered for children who need it.

Motor Activities — Goal: Walk slowly with balance and control carrying water.
Activity: Children will carry a cup of water slowly across the 'desert' (a winding tape path), trying not to spill a drop, and pour it onto our class succulent at the finish.
Materials: Cups; water tray; tape path; class succulent
Grouping: Small groups — classroom; teacher-supervised
Support: A marked halfway 'rest oasis' spot for children who need a break point.

Technology — Goal: Watch a desert flower bloom in time-lapse video.
Activity: We will watch a short teacher-selected time-lapse of a cactus flower opening — a bloom that takes hours squeezed into a minute — and gasp-count how many petals we can see.
Materials: Projector; teacher-selected time-lapse clip
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A front seat so the fast bloom is easy to see; the clip replayed once for anyone who missed it.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Repot and care for a real desert plant.
Activity: We will plant our class succulent into a bigger pot outdoors (teacher guides hands away from any prickles; this succulent is spine-free), water it, and choose its sunny home spot together.
Materials: Succulent (spine-free); pot; soil; watering can
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A small, light pot to carry with a partner for children who need support.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Build perseverance: growing even in hard places.
Activity: A cactus grows very slowly in a hard, dry place — and still blooms. We will talk about growing even when something is hard, and name one thing we keep practicing even though it is slow.
Materials: Cactus photo; feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Specific praise that names persistence when a child shares.

title: Desert / Egypt: Pyramids and the Nile
subject: Social Studies
description: Preschool day plan from the 'Desert / Egypt' thematic week (May): Pyramids and the Nile. Focus book: A Trip to Ancient Egypt — — a picture book introducing ancient Egypt — pyramids, the Nile River, and life long ago (substitute any age-appropriate ancient Egypt title on hand). Ten connected activities across literacy, science, social studies, math, art, music and movement, motor skills, technology, outdoor learning, and a life-lesson moment — each with a goal, materials, grouping, and a built-in support strategy so every child can join in.
evidence:
Focus book: A Trip to Ancient Egypt — — a picture book introducing ancient Egypt — pyramids, the Nile River, and life long ago (substitute any age-appropriate ancient Egypt title on hand)

Language Arts — Goal: Learn about long-ago Egypt and sequence how a pyramid was built.
Activity: We will read about Egypt long ago and add words to our wall: pyramid, Nile, pharaoh (a king from long ago). Children will sequence picture cards of building a pyramid: cut stone, pull stone, stack stone.
Materials: Focus book; word cards; sequence cards
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Word cards with real photos and a chance to say each word with a partner first.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Test ramps and discover they make moving heavy things easier.
Activity: Children will test moving a heavy block: pull it across the floor, then pull it up a ramp board. We will talk about how ramps made the work easier for the pyramid builders long ago.
Materials: Wooden blocks; ramp boards; smooth floor
Grouping: Small groups — science table/floor
Support: A hand-over-hand start from the teacher for children learning to roll the block up.

Social Science — Goal: Locate Egypt and the Nile and explain why the river mattered.
Activity: We will find Egypt on the globe, trace the Nile River with a finger, and talk about how the river gave water for farms and boats for travel — a river can be like a road.
Materials: Globe; focus book map page
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A pointer partner to take the globe journey together.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Count down layers to build a pyramid pattern.
Activity: Working in teams, children will build block pyramids by counting layers: a row of 5, then 4, then 3, then 2, then 1 on top — counting down as the pyramid grows up.
Materials: Unit blocks; layer number cards
Grouping: Centers — building area; teacher-guided demo first
Support: A layer guide strip showing how many blocks each row needs for children building with support.

Creative Art — Goal: Collage a pyramid scene using triangles.
Activity: Children will build a pyramid collage from triangles: a big sand-colored triangle, a blue Nile river strip beside it, a sun, and triangle details glued in rows like stones.
Materials: Triangle cutouts; blue strips; glue; background paper
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: Pre-cut triangles in two sizes for children still learning scissor control.

Music / Movement — Goal: Row cooperatively to a song's tempo.
Activity: We will sit in two lines facing a partner, hold hands, and rock back and forth 'rowing on the Nile' while singing a gentle rowing song, speeding up and slowing with the 'current.'
Materials: Teacher-led rowing song; open rug space
Grouping: Large group — rug; teacher-led
Support: Paired rowing with the teacher for children learning the rhythm.

Motor Activities — Goal: Pull, carry, and place blocks in a builder relay.
Activity: Children will be pyramid builders: haul a foam block on a 'sled' (a mat) to the building site, carry it up the ramp, and place it on our growing class pyramid, then return for the next.
Materials: Foam blocks; mat sleds; ramp; pyramid base outline
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: Foam blocks only and a short hauling distance for safety and success.

Technology — Goal: View real pyramids through photographs and compare scale.
Activity: We will look at projected photographs of the real pyramids and the Nile today (teacher-selected) and compare their size to people and camels standing nearby.
Materials: Projector; teacher-selected photos
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Front seats and a freeze-frame moment for children to look longer at one pyramid.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Build and compare sand pyramids outdoors.
Activity: In the sandbox, children will build sand pyramids with molds and wet sand, testing which stands tallest, then build a blue-scarf 'Nile' beside their pyramid city.
Materials: Sandbox; pyramid molds; buckets; blue scarf
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: Sturdier pre-made molds for children whose freehand pyramids crumble.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Value teamwork and perseverance in big jobs.
Activity: No one builds a pyramid alone — it takes thousands of helping hands over many years. We will talk about our own class projects that only work when everyone helps, and thank our helpers by name (classmates can be thanked with kind words).
Materials: Pyramid photo; feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: Sentence frame ('Together we can...') for support.

title: Desert / Egypt: Picture Writing Celebration
subject: Social Studies

evidence:
Focus book: Writing with Pictures — — a simple picture book about hieroglyphs — the picture writing of ancient Egypt (substitute any picture-writing title on hand)

Language Arts — Goal: Compose a message using picture symbols (early writing).
Activity: We will learn that Egyptians wrote with pictures called hieroglyphs. Children will 'write' a message on a paper scroll by choosing symbols for their ideas (sun = day, eye = see, heart = love) and dictate their message for the teacher to write below.

Grouping: Small groups — tables; teacher-guided
Support: A symbol bank tray in front of them so choosing is easy; dictation done one-to-one quietly with the teacher.

Science / Nature Studies — Goal: Compare how writing tools work on different papers.
Activity: Children will test writing on different papers — thin, thick, rough (sandpaper-backed is teacher-handled only as a display), glossy — and discover which paper holds marker and crayon best, like papyrus held ink.
Materials: Paper samples; markers; crayons
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: A partner to test with and thicker paper offered first for an early success.

Social Science — Goal: Review and sort learning from the whole theme.
Activity: We will review our whole theme by sorting picture cards: 'from the desert,' 'from Egypt long ago,' and 'things we share with both' (needing water, telling stories, helping family).
Materials: Review picture cards; three sorting mats
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: A 'long ago / like us' picture sort with fewer cards for children building the idea.

Cognitive Skills & Math — Goal: Build and count a repeating pattern with symbols.
Activity: Children will create a pattern border for their scroll using picture symbols (eye, sun, eye, sun...) and count how many symbols fit along the edge of their paper.
Materials: Symbol stamps/cards; long paper strips
Grouping: Centers — math/art area; child-led after demo
Support: A three-symbol pattern starter for children new to longer patterns.

Creative Art — Goal: Finish a decorated 'scroll' combining the week's art.
Activity: Children will finish their scrolls: gold paint (teacher-dispensed) dabbed on the edges, their week's pyramid collage attached, and their picture-symbol message pressed in the center.
Materials: Scroll papers; gold paint; pyramid collages; glue
Grouping: Art center, groups of 4–5
Support: A larger-edged scroll and thicker brushes for easier handling.

Music / Movement — Goal: Celebrate with a scarf parade responding to music changes.
Activity: Our celebration parade will wind around the room with scarves waving like festival banners, dancing fast 'river' steps and slow 'desert' steps as the music changes.
Materials: Scarves; recorded music
Grouping: Large group; teacher-led
Support: A place beside the teacher in the parade line for cueing.

Motor Activities — Goal: Carry carefully, then hold a still pose with control.
Activity: In our messenger relay, children will carry a scroll carefully overhead to the 'temple' mat, freeze in a sphinx pose (lying on tummies, chins up) for three counts, then hurry back to tag the next messenger.
Materials: Paper scrolls; mats; cones
Grouping: Small groups — movement area; teacher-supervised
Support: A shorter relay route and the scroll carried with a partner.

Technology — Goal: Document our work with photos and view our week's slideshow.
Activity: We will photograph our scrolls and pyramid art with the teacher's help, then watch the Desert/Egypt week slideshow and find our own work on the big screen.
Materials: Tablet (teacher-held); projector; week's photos
Grouping: Large group; teacher-led
Support: Front seats and a pause on their own work for children who want a longer look.

Outdoor Education — Goal: Share our work in an outdoor celebration by our pretend Nile.
Activity: We will hold our celebration outdoors: sit on blankets beside a blue-sheet 'Nile,' share our scrolls with a partner, and read the picture messages to each other like storytellers long ago.
Materials: Blankets; blue sheet; finished scrolls
Grouping: Whole class — outdoors; teacher-led
Support: A blanket buddy and their scroll already placed at their spot to reduce carrying load.

Life Lesson Library — Goal: Connect with people across time: we share feelings and stories.
Activity: We will close the theme noticing that people long ago told stories, loved their families, and helped each other — just like us. Each child will share one way people long ago are the same as us.
Materials: Scrolls; feelings chart
Grouping: Large group — carpet; teacher-led
Support: The option to read their scroll's symbols instead of a spoken reflection.

Language Arts — Goal: Retell the caterpillar's story in sequence using time words.

Materials: Insect models; spider model; magnifiers; photos
Grouping: Small groups — science table
Support: A song strip with body-part pictures for children to check their count.

Activity: We will talk about where we see bugs — at the park, in the garden, at home — and how people and bugs share the same world, each needing their own space and food.
